activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In England and Wales, a landlord must place a tenant's deposit in a government-backed protection scheme within 30 days of receiving it.
story:
The open house on Caldwell Street smelled of lemon polish and fresh paint, which Jade understood immediately as a performance, the way a biology poster of a cell is a performance, everything sorted into its phylum and labeled neatly while the real thing is messier and alive. Her mother had brought her along because Jade was "good with numbers," a reputation earned the year she caught a billing error on the family phone plan, and because her mother wanted a second set of eyes before committing to anything. The agent, a woman in a gray blazer, had already begun to expatiate on the kitchen's quartz countertops, the subway tile, the "enviable morning light," and Jade let the words wash past while she studied the printed sheet in her hand.

The sheet listed the price, which was not a price but a kind of wager. Her mother had explained some of it on the drive over: you did not pay the whole amount, you borrowed most of it, and the loan was called a mortgage, and you paid it back over decades with interest stacked on top like snow that never melted. Jade had done quiet arithmetic in the passenger seat. The monthly payment on this house, even with a sizable down payment, would be more than what her mother currently paid for their flat, more by a margin that made her stomach feel thin and diaphanous, like tissue paper held up to a window.

Paulina arrived with her father ten minutes later, waving at Jade across the hallway with the exaggerated enthusiasm of someone delighted to find a familiar face in a room full of strangers. Paulina's father was looking at the same houses for the opposite reason; they rented, and their landlord was selling, and they needed somewhere before autumn. "We have to scrape together a deposit," Paulina said when they retreated together into the narrow back garden, which was mostly paving stones and one determined hydrangea. "Two months of rent up front, apparently. And then you just hope you get it back someday."

"That's a lot of money to hand to someone you don't know," Jade said.

"Right? That's what Mekhi said." Paulina pulled out her phone. Mekhi had moved to Manchester in June, before year twelve started, and he still messaged the group chat at odd hours. She held the screen toward Jade. He had written: paid my deposit weeks ago, never got any paperwork about it, is that normal? does it just vanish into the landlord's pocket?

Jade looked at the message for a long moment. Something about it snagged, the way a loose thread snags. She had spent the morning learning how buying worked, the down payment, the mortgage, the slow transfer of a house from one name to another, and it struck her that renting had its own architecture of trust, and that trust needed a structure around it or it was just a leap. She did not know what that structure was. She suspected, from the confident way Mekhi's landlord had pocketed the transfer and gone silent, that there was meant to be one.

Inside, Mr. Otieno from number fourteen had drifted in to look, partly nosy and partly serious, as he put it. He owned his flat outright, having finished his mortgage "before you were born, girls," and Jade asked him, feeling her way, whether a landlord in England could just keep a deposit in his own account. Mr. Otieno rubbed his chin. "There's a rule about that," he said. "A landlord has to put the deposit in a government-backed protection scheme within 30 days of getting it." He shrugged, as if to say that was all he remembered, and went back to examining the boiler.

Jade took out her phone and typed it back to Mekhi, word for word as Mr. Otieno had said it: within 30 days, government-backed protection scheme. Then she added: ask the landlord for the paperwork. If he hasn't done it, that's not normal. She stood in the hallway while it sent, the message spinning out toward Manchester, past the agent who was now expatiating on the loft conversion to a couple who nodded without asking about the roof.

In the garden again, her mother found her. "Well?" her mother said. "Worth putting an offer in?" Jade looked at the hydrangea, at Paulina and her father conferring by the fence over their own arithmetic, at her phone where Mekhi's reply had already arrived, three question marks followed by "calling him now." Her mother wanted certainty. Jade had two ledgers in her head now, the mortgage and its patient decades, the deposit and its thirty days, and she could hold both at once without pretending either was simple.

"I think we should look at three more before we decide," she said, and her mother laughed, surprised, and put an arm around her shoulders as they walked back through the lemon-polish smell toward the car.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Psychologist George Bonanno's research on bereaved people found that resilience is common, and that there are no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss.
story:
Kevin stood at the sink rinsing his grandmother's teacup, the one with the hairline crack she had refused to throw out, and realized he could not remember whether it went on the second shelf or the third. His mother was at the funeral home again. His father was at the table with the bills the flowers had generated, writing checks in the careful hand of a man postponing something. The kitchen smelled like the casseroles neighbors had been leaving on the porch since Tuesday, and Kevin had not cried since the morning they told him, and that fact sat in him like a stone he was afraid to swallow.

"You're still coming Friday," Dean said on the phone, not asking. "Raquel's already got the tickets."

"I don't know. Is that weird? Like, my grandmother died four days ago."

"So come or don't come. But don't not come because you think you're supposed to be doing something else."

Kevin hung up and put the teacup on the second shelf, then moved it to the third, then back.

He had gone to school on Wednesday. He had laughed at Raquel's impression of their calculus teacher before first period, a real laugh, loud, and then caught himself in the hallway afterward as if he'd shoplifted something. Ms. Dela Cruz had stopped him by the water fountain, asked how he was, and he'd said fine, and she'd looked at him one beat too long before letting him go. He kept replaying the laugh. Somewhere he had absorbed the idea that grief had stations, that everyone passed through them in order, and that skipping a station meant the ticket was invalid, that the sorrow would come collect him later with interest.

The flashback arrived while he was microwaving his father's coffee, which had gone cold at the table. His grandmother's kitchen, two summers ago, the window open to the sound of the sprinkler next door. She was teaching him to make her soup, the one with the lemon and egg, and he'd asked why she whisked so long and she'd said because your grandfather never had the patience, and then she'd laughed at her own cruelty to a dead man, a full-throated laugh that had embarrassed him then. He'd thought it was strange, her laughing about a husband eight years gone. He had been sixteen and had filed it under things old people did.

The microwave beeped. His father took the cup without looking up and said, "Thank you," and Kevin sat across from him and finally said it out loud.

"I don't think I'm doing this right."

His father's pen stopped. "Doing what."

"Grieving. I laughed at school today. At a joke. Wednesday, I mean. I'm sleeping fine. I keep waiting to fall apart and it's not happening." He heard how it sounded, like a complaint about good weather.

His father turned a check over, wrote the amount on the back, and slid it into an envelope. "Your grandfather, when his sister died, he planted the whole garden in one weekend. People said he was in denial. He just liked the garden." He looked up. "I cry at the drop of a hat. That's mine. You'll have your own thing, or you won't, and neither one of them is a report card."

That night Kevin took his laptop to bed, meaning to email his English teacher, and instead found himself typing the words into the search bar. He read for an hour. A psychologist named George Bonanno had followed bereaved people over time, and the finding that surfaced again and again across the studies was not what the posters in the counselor's office had implied. Resilience was common. That was the actual result, stated plainly, and beyond it, a second finding, the one that undid the stone in his chest: there were no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss. No universal sequence. He read it three times, waiting to find the catch, the instruction, the correct procedure he'd missed. There wasn't one. The somnolence that had been pressing on him since Tuesday loosened, though he noticed he still couldn't tell whether what he felt was relief or just fatigue finally allowed to be fatigue.

Friday, the concert was in a converted warehouse, and Raquel found him beforehand at the food trucks, holding two lemonades he hadn't asked for. "You look cerebral," she said, meaning his face. "Stop that."

"I'm not being cerebral. I read something."

"Read what?"

"This guy studied people after someone died. Actual people, over time. Turns out being okay isn't a malfunction. Resilience is common. And there are no mandatory stages everyone has to pass through." He heard himself reciting it and worried it sounded like a lecture, like he'd swallowed a pamphlet. "It's not that I don't miss her," he added, quieter.

Raquel took her lemonade. "Obviously you miss her. You named the soup."

He hadn't realized he'd told them about the soup, but he had, in the fall, when he'd made it wrong in the dorm kitchen at the college visit weekend and Dean had eaten two bowls anyway. The band started inside, a wall of sound from the loading doors, and people moved toward it, and Kevin moved with them.

He stood near the back with his friends, and during the third song a slow one, an unexpected slow one, a lyric about a kitchen window caught somewhere in his throat, and he let it sit there, hot and unswallowed, and did nothing about it. He didn't cry. He didn't not cry. He put his hand on Dean's shoulder to steady himself against the crowd, and drank the lemonade, which was more sour than sweet, and stayed until the last chord rang out over the warehouse floor and the lights came up on everyone's faces at once.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, wearing a seat belt reduces serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half.
story:
Payton had the car keys in her fist before Mr. Korhonen even reached the driveway, which he noticed, and which he said nothing about. He was the neighbour from four houses down, retired from something he never specified, and her mother had arranged the whole thing over the fence while Payton was at swim practice. The car was her mother's, a gray sedan with a crack across the windshield that her mother called character. Payton had read the driver's manual twice, cover to cover, and could recite the right-of-way rules at intersections she had never seen.

"Seat belt," Mr. Korhonen said, once he had lowered himself into the passenger seat with a small grunt.

Payton turned the key. The engine caught, and she was already reaching for the gearshift when he put his hand flat on the dashboard. She looked at him. He looked at her lap, where the belt was not.

"I'm in the driveway," she said. "We're going ten feet."

"Wearing a seat belt reduces serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half," he said. "Half. And you're wearing none of it." He settled back and crossed his arms, which made his seat belt lock and have to be pulled out again, slowly, an inch at a time. She watched him fight with it, and she understood that they were going to sit in this driveway until she did the thing she had already been taught to do.

She pulled the belt across. It clicked. "Fine," she said, and said nothing else, because she was thinking about her father, who drove without his belt on the short trips, to the store, to her grandmother's, a habit he described with a shrug and the phrase you can't plan everything. She had grown up half-believing that, the way you absorb a smell in a house. Her friend Esther believed the opposite and loudly, was the sort of person who cited statistics at lunch, and Payton had always filed that under things Esther does, alongside the veganism and the petitions.

They pulled out of the driveway. Mr. Korhonen directed her down the street, past the crepuscular hush of the cul-de-sac where the streetlights had just come on, and out onto the wider road, and Payton found that her hands knew things her brain did not. She checked the mirror without deciding to. She braked at the stop sign before he told her to. When a dog ran out from between two parked cars and she stopped short, both of them pitched forward against their belts, and Mr. Korhonen grunted again, and Payton started laughing in a way that felt like it was coming from somewhere deeper than the joke deserved.

"Your belt just incapacitated you," she said. "You couldn't fly through the windshield."

"That's the general idea," he said, rubbing his collarbone.

"Half," she said. "It's not everything. It's half." She said it out loud to hear how it sounded, because her father's version, the shrug, and Esther's version, the certainty, had never fit together in her head, and this number did something to both of them. Half meant the belt wasn't a promise. Half also meant that the shrug was a lie, that not wearing it wasn't acceptance of chaos, it was just a worse bet dressed up as philosophy. She didn't say any of this. She signaled, checked her blind spot, and turned back toward her street, where the porch light was on and her mother was standing at the end of the driveway with the dog on a leash, waving.

Mr. Korhonen had her pull in, straight, and set the brake. "Not bad," he said. "Same time Thursday." He got out, then leaned back down to the window. "Tell your father," he said, and tapped his own shoulder where the belt had crossed it, and walked off up the sidewalk before she could ask how he knew.

Payton sat in the parked car with the engine off and the belt still on, and watched her mother coming toward the driver's side, and did not take it off yet.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A necessary condition must hold for something to happen but may not be enough: the sun being above the horizon is necessary for direct sunlight, but not sufficient, since something may cast a shadow.
story:
Ms. Barrett had written one word on the board, "Conditions," and underlined it twice, and Emily could not stop touching the envelope in the front pocket of her backpack, which had been sitting there since breakfast, sealed, with the early admission logo faintly visible through the paper when she tilted it toward the window light.

"If you get straight A's, you're in," Ronan said. He had his feet under Bruno's chair, which was how he argued, sprawled, as though certainty were a matter of surface area. "That's the whole system. Grades in, acceptance out."

"That's not how it works and you know it," Bruno said. "There are people with perfect transcripts who don't get in."

"Then the system is broken."

"Or your argument is."

Ms. Barrett let them go at it, wandering between the desks with her coffee, and Emily watched Ronan's confidence calcify in real time, his posture stiffening each time Bruno scored, until he was sitting almost straight, arms crossed, defending a position he had clearly adopted that morning and would probably abandon by lunch. The classroom smelled of whiteboard marker and the radiator's burnt dust. Outside, the October sun was low over the parking lot, and the flagpole threw a long shadow across three rows of cars.

"Okay," Ms. Barrett said finally. "Ronan, draw it. If grades guarantee admission, what does the arrow look like?"

Ronan went to the board and drew A's, then an arrow, then a big letter with a checkmark. "Grades, therefore in."

"And what did Bruno say exists?"

"People who have the A's and didn't get in."

"So the arrow breaks," Bruno said from his seat. "One counterexample."

Ronan stood at the board with the marker going slack in his hand. "Fine, then what, grades count for nothing?"

"No," Emily said, and was surprised at herself, because she had been quiet for twenty minutes and had not planned to speak, not with the envelope pressing against her notebooks like a held breath. But the whole argument had been circling something she actually knew about, in her hands, unopened. "There's a middle thing. Something can be required without being enough."

Ms. Barrett turned. "Go on."

Emily stood, took the marker from Ronan, and drew a horizon line, then a sun above it, then a stick figure with a shadow stretched out to the side. "The sun has to be above the horizon for there to be direct sunlight. That part has to hold. But it's not enough, because something can still cast a shadow. The sun being up doesn't guarantee you're standing in the light."

Ronan squinted at the drawing. "So grades are like the sun."

"Grades are like the horizon," Bruno said. "No, wait."

"Grades are like the sun being up," Emily said. "You can't get in without them, or at least it's very hard, and everyone knows that. But you can have them and still end up in a shadow you didn't choose. Something else is blocking it and you don't always get to see what."

Ms. Barrett wrote "necessary" above the horizon line and "sufficient" to the side of the shadow. "Emily just gave us the distinction. Necessary: it must hold. Sufficient: it's enough on its own. Now, is anything in admissions sufficient? Anyone?"

Ronan said legacy, and someone said a Nobel Prize, and the discussion rolled forward into hypotheticals, whether a perfect essay could be sufficient, whether being a recruited athlete was necessary for anything at all, and Emily sat back down with her ears warm and did not hear most of it. Because the problem was not Ronan's argument anymore. The problem was that she had spent two years treating her average like a promise, like a signed contract with the admissions office, and she had told her mother, in the car, that it was basically decided, and her mother had said that's wonderful, Emily, and now the envelope was in the bag and the sun was up and the flagpole's shadow had moved two parking spaces since the period began.

Brunon leaned across the aisle during the transition to pair work. "You okay? You went somewhere."

"I'm fine."

"You did that whole sun thing like you were building a case," he said. "Like a lawyer who already knows the verdict."

She looked at him. He was one of the only people who had applied to the same program, and he had a 91 where she had a 97, and until this morning she had felt a small private shame about how much that difference had pleased her, which was a congenital flaw of hers, she thought, wanting to be ahead, born with it the way some people were born with crooked teeth. "It's not a verdict," she said. "That was the whole point. Grades are necessary. Not sufficient."

"Right, but you said it like you were convincing yourself."

The bell was in four minutes. Ms. Barrett was assigning the response paragraph, necessary versus sufficient in your own life, due Thursday, and the class was already zipping bags. Emily took the envelope out. She turned it over twice, ran her thumb under the flap, and stopped, because Ronan was watching from two seats over, and Bruno was watching from one, and the classroom had gone narrow and very bright.

"You want us to look away?" Ronan said.

"No," Emily said. "I want a witness."

She tore it open. The letter was one page, and she read the first line, and then the second, and her face did something she could not control, and Bruno said, quietly, "What's it say?"

Emily folded the page in half and put it inside her notebook, under the page where she had copied the horizon, the sun, and the long thin shadow reaching away from the stick figure toward the edge of the frame.

"It says the sun is up," she said, and started packing her bag.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: The force on a charge in an electric field equals the charge times the field strength, F = qE, so doubling the charge doubles the force.
story:
The physics lab smelled of warm dust and the lemon cleaner the janitor used on counters nobody used. Emily sat at the third bench with her workbook open to problem twelve, the one Ms. Balogun had circled twice in red pen, and tried to pretend the circling meant nothing.

Between the two charged plates, the field was supposed to be uniform. That was the gift of the setup, the whole reason it appeared on every exam: you could compute E from the potential difference and the separation, and then the number you held was true everywhere in the gap. Emily had done the first part an hour ago, in the margin of her notes, and gotten a field of four thousand newtons per coulomb. She had underlined it twice, the way Ms. Balogun underlined things, and then she had gone no further, because the second part of the problem asked about a dust particle carrying a charge of three nanocoulombs, and Emily had no intuition for what a nanocoulomb felt like. Nothing in her life had prepared her to imagine one.

Zavier dropped his bag on the bench across from her and began copying the diagram off the board without asking whether she minded. He never minded about things, or if he did, he converted the minding into a sardonic comment and let it go. "You're staring at it like it owes you money," he said.

"It's the dust particle. I can do the field. I can't do the particle."

"Then you're a neophyte same as me." He said it cheerfully, as though the word were a club he had just discovered they both belonged to. "Marie-Eve finished, though. She's been finished since three o'clock."

Marie-Eve was by the window with her workbook closed, watching the parking lot the way she did on Thursdays, when her mother came late. She was the kind of student who made the rest of the room feel rehearsed. Emily remembered the first week of September, when she had chosen the third bench specifically to be near Zavier and far from the window, a decision she now weighed whenever the afternoon light made the equations on the board hard to read. She had traded visibility for company, and some days that seemed wise and other days it seemed like the small cowardice that dressed itself up as strategy.

She pulled the workbook closer and read the problem again. A dust particle, charge three nanocoulombs, sitting at rest between the plates. Find the force on it. The field was four thousand newtons per coulomb. She wrote F equals, and then stopped, because the charge and the field were sitting next to each other in her notes like two strangers at a bus stop, and nothing in her told her how they combined.

"Do you multiply or is it one of those inverse things," she said, not quite a question.

Zavier looked up with his pen in his mouth. "If it were inverse, doubling the charge would halve the force, and that would be a stupid universe."

That was how he reasoned, by deciding what the universe owed him, and the infuriating part was how often it worked. Emily sat with the sentence anyway, turning it over. Doubling the charge doubled the force. She tested it against the formula Ms. Balogun had written on the board in the first week and never taken down: F equals q times E. If E stayed four thousand and q grew from three nanocoulombs to six, the force would go from whatever it was to twice whatever it was. The charge and the field multiplied. That was the whole mechanic, simple and unfair in its simplicity, like discovering a door she had been leaning on opened outward.

She did the arithmetic on the back of her hand first, then properly in the margin. Twelve micronewtons. She said it out loud before she could doubt it. "Twelve micronewtons. That's the push on the dust."

Marie-Eve turned from the window. "That's what I got. Zavier, you're still on the diagram."

"Zavier is a neophyte," Zavier said. "Zavier contains multitudes, and none of them can find the force on a particle."

"But why twelve," Emily said, because getting the right answer without the reason had destabilized something in her; the number sat in her hand like money she hadn't earned. "If the particle carried six nanocoulombs instead of three, would it be twenty-four?"

"Double the charge, double the force," Marie-Eve said. She said it flatly, a thing she had already settled. Then, quieter, "My mom's not here yet either."

Emily looked at her own page. Twelve micronewtons was almost nothing, a force smaller than the weight of a grain of rice, and yet it came out of the same arithmetic that described lightning. She held both of those facts at once and could not make them the same size in her mind. Maybe that was the actual lesson, though nobody had assigned it: that the equations were indifferent to scale, and the indifference was hers to interpret. Or maybe she was wrong, and tomorrow Ms. Balogun would circle something else in red.

She checked the sign of her answer. The particle was positive, the top plate was positive, so the push pointed down, toward the negative plate, and she drew the arrow carefully, darker than the other lines.

Ms. Balogun passed behind them on her way to the door, paused at Emily's margin, and moved on without a word. Emily watched her go, then flipped to the next problem, where a smaller charge waited in the same field, and began.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: In Judaism, a day begins at sundown, so a Seder or a Sabbath dinner is held on the evening that starts the holiday, not the evening that ends it.
story:
Keira's grandmother had led the Seder for thirty-one years, and this year, before the arthritis won the argument, she had pressed the Haggadah into Keira's hands and said, "Yours now. Don't drop it, it's older than your mother." Which was how Keira came to spend the week before Passover with a stack of index cards, a borrowed timer, and the growing suspicion that she had made a terrible mistake with the hall.

The family had outgrown her grandmother's apartment somewhere around cousin number nine, so Keira had booked the community hall down the street for Friday evening. She had checked the calendar, counted the days, and reserved the room with the confidence of a person who had not yet learned to distrust her own arithmetic. On Tuesday her grandmother called, and between asking whether Keira had bought enough horseradish and whether anyone had reminded her uncle to bring the wine, she said, "So, the hall, you have it for the first night?"

"Friday," Keira said. "The fifteenth."

A pause travelled down the line, long enough for Keira to hear her grandmother's kettle whistling somewhere behind her. "The fifteenth starts Thursday night," her grandmother said, and then, before Keira could ask, "I'm not explaining it, you'll work it out. Ask your mother. No, don't ask your mother, she'll get it wrong too. Look it up."

Keira looked it up. She sat at the kitchen table with her laptop open and a piece of parsley she'd been meaning to chop, and read it three times. In Judaism, a day begins at sundown, so the Seder was held on the evening that started the holiday, not the evening that ended it. She read it aloud to the parsley. The parsley was unmoved, but Keira sat back, half delighted and half indignant, because she had been walking around for sixteen years assuming days began when her phone said they did, at midnight, or when her alarm went off, whichever came first and was worse. An entire day had been starting at sundown this whole time, without her permission.

Then came the practical problem, which was that she had booked the hall for the wrong evening. She called the hall office on Wednesday, beseeching the volunteer who answered in her most reasonable voice, and the volunteer said the hall was taken Thursday by a quilting group whose leader, the cashier at the hardware store had told her, was not a woman to be trifled with. Keira offered a remittance of the fee, a transfer of the deposit, anything, and the volunteer said, "Honey, I can't move the quilters. They've got a waiting list."

So the Seder would have to happen at her grandmother's apartment after all, which meant chairs, which meant folding tables from the church basement, which meant Keira and her friend Keon hauling furniture up two flights of stairs on Thursday afternoon while her grandmother directed from a kitchen stool like a small, satisfied general. Keon, who was not Jewish and had volunteered mostly for the food, kept asking questions. "So the holiday starts tonight? At sundown? Not tomorrow?"

"At sundown," Keira said. "The evening that starts it, not the evening that ends it."

"That's so much better than midnight," Keon said, setting down his end of the table. "Nobody's awake at midnight. Sundown, everyone's awake, everyone's hungry."

George arrived with the ceremonial eggs and a box of matzah he had carried on the bus like it was a sleeping infant, and by the time the sun went down the apartment was full, and loud, and smelled of soup. Keira stood at the head of the table with the Haggadah, which was indeed older than her mother, and discovered that thirty-one years of Seders had not transferred themselves into her index cards. She asked the Four Questions in a voice that cracked once, on the second question, which her uncle applauded as if she had hit a high note on purpose.

She made mistakes. She skipped a blessing and had to go back; she poured Elijah's cup with such enthusiasm that it overflowed onto the good tablecloth, and her grandmother said, "Elijah is a tidy man, Keira," and the whole table laughed, and Keira laughed too, because it was a joke and also, she suspected, a small correction she would remember forever. Somewhere in the middle of the meal, her uncle grew torpid with brisket and began narrating a dream he'd had about a talking doorbell, and Keira let him, because a leader, she was learning, is partly a person who knows when to yield the floor.

What she could not work out, even by the end, was whether she had actually led anything or merely stood at the front while the family led itself, the way it had for thirty-one years, with or without a grandmother at the head. She turned this over while she hid the afikoman under the sofa cushion, and Keon found it in under a minute because he had watched her do it, and he claimed his prize, a dollar from her uncle, with the smugness of a man who understood the system.

Her grandmother caught her hand as the table was being cleared. "Next year," she said, "book the hall for Thursday."

"I know," Keira said. "Sundown. The evening that starts it."

"And buy more horseradish. Your uncle wept like a child and it wasn't even the strong kind."

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: Keeping money as cash has an opportunity cost: the interest or returns it could have earned in a savings account or investment.
story:
The appointment had been made for something else entirely, a schedule change that had since resolved itself, but Madison sat down in Mr. Levy's office anyway because she had walked all the way there and because the thing she actually wanted to say had been riding shotgun in her head for three days. She put her phone on his desk, screen up, showing the listing: a 2004 hatchback, silver, 3,200 dollars, a private seller two towns over. Mr. Levy swiveled his chair, looked at the phone, then at her, and waited in the way counselors waited, which she found either generous or lazy depending on the day.

"I have the money," she said. "I've been saving since I was fourteen. Birthday money, the farm stand, last summer at the pool. It's in a jar in my closet." She had counted it twice on Sunday night, sitting cross-legged on her bed, bills fanned out like cards she was afraid to play.

Mr. Levy asked what the money had been for, originally, and Madison said a car, mostly, which was true, but the word "mostly" came out louder than she intended. The original plan had been simpler when she was fourteen. Now she was sixteen and the money sat at a fork.

The complication had a name, and the name had a face. Derrick worked at the credit union after school, filing paperwork and occasionally explaining things to people even though nobody official had asked him to. On Tuesday he had looked at her across the cafeteria table, pushing his tray aside, and said, "Cash in a jar earns nothing. Keeping money as cash has an opportunity cost, the interest or returns it could have earned in a savings account or investment. That's the whole thing, that's what it's called." He had learned it that morning, apparently, from a pamphlet, and he recited it with the conviction of someone who wanted to be lionized for knowing it, which Ethen, sitting beside him, punctured immediately by saying the pamphlet was sitting in the break room and anyone could read it.

"It's real, though," Derrick had said, undeterred. "You put the money in the account, the account pays you for keeping it there. Your jar pays you dust."

In Mr. Levy's office, Madison laid out both futures the way he had taught them to do in sophomore planning seminars, except this time it wasn't hypothetical. In one version she owned the hatchback by Friday and drove herself to the farm stand and the pool and, come autumn, to the community college campus for the dual enrollment chemistry course she'd been accepted into, the one that met at 7:40 in the morning, forty minutes before any school bus arrived. In the other version the money sat in an account earning whatever accounts earned, small amounts arriving like a tide that never quite reached her ankles, and she rode the bus to chemistry and got there late or not at all, and the jar in her closet stayed full, which felt like safety and also like nothing happening.

Mr. Levy did not tell her which to choose. He asked her what the bus schedule actually said, and she admitted she hadn't looked, and he slid his computer monitor toward her so she could. The earliest bus got there at 7:55. She stared at that number for a while.

"You're not deciding between a car and money," he said finally, which she thought at first was going to become one of those trenchant counselor pronouncements, except he stopped there, and she realized the sentence was incomplete on purpose. She finished it herself, quietly. She was deciding between a car and what the money could become, and also between the money and what the car could make possible, and both of those were true at once, which was the part nobody's pamphlet covered.

She asked him, almost hoping he would, whether one was objectively better, and he said people wrote whole books arguing both sides, that every choice had a price tag on the thing you didn't pick, and that sixteen was not too early to learn to look at that tag honestly. She suspected he said some version of this to everyone, in every stratum of the school, the honors kids and the kids on the late bus alike, and that it still counted.

Outside his office, in the hallway that smelled like floor wax and rain jackets, she texted Derrick from the bench by the trophy case. How much does the account actually pay, she typed, and then, before he could answer, typed again: and is the guy with the hatchback still doing test drives Thursday. She looked up at the glass doors, the wet parking lot, the long walk home that would take forty minutes in the rain. Her thumb hovered over the send arrow.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The FAFSA is the form US students complete to apply for federal financial aid such as Pell Grants and federal loans, and many states and colleges also use it to award their own aid.
story:
The campus tour began under a banner that read Admitted Students Day, which was not quite true for Mia, who was still waiting, and she felt the falseness of it in her shoulders as she joined the group outside the library. Sonia had gotten in early, in December, and walked beside her now with the loose ease of someone whose future had already voted. Aspen was somewhere ahead, taking photographs of the quad as though the bricks might change before April.

"Make it real in your head," Sonia said. "That's what my mom keeps telling me. Walk around like you live here." Mia tried. She noted the dining hall, the mediocre fountain, the lecture hall where a professor was holding the door for a skateboard. She wanted the place with a plainness that surprised her, the way you want water only when you cannot reach it.

Their guide, a junior with a laminated lanyard, led them past the financial aid office, a squat brick building with a short line already forming outside it at ten in the morning. "Even on a Saturday," Sonia said. Mia filed the image away without knowing why.

At the lunch table in the student union, Aspen spread out brochures like a magistrate laying out evidence, weighing each school's virtues with mock solemnity, and the table laughed. But when Mia laughed too, the laugh had an edge to it, because for her the verdict was not hers to deliver. She caught herself wanting to introspect, to sit quietly and sort out what she actually felt, and equally wanting not to, because what she felt might not matter. A deferred decision is a strange thing; it teaches you to keep two futures alive at once, like a pianist practicing with both hands on two different pianos.

Ms. Goh, her neighbor back home, had told her something once that she kept returning to: that the wanting itself is information. Mia hadn't understood it then. She wasn't sure she understood it now, walking under the elms with her tour lanyard flapping, but the sentence followed her around the quad like a small dog.

That night, back in her bedroom, her mother called her down to the kitchen. The laptop's light was the only light; it was past eleven, and her mother had her glasses pushed up into her hair. "I started the forms," her mother said. "Your counselor sent the link a month ago and I kept putting it off."

"What forms?" Mia pulled a chair around so they could both see the screen.

"It's the FAFSA," Mia said slowly, reading the header. "The form for federal financial aid, Pell Grants and federal loans." The page scrolled under her mother's careful finger. Further down, a line about state and college aid stopped them both. "Wait. It says states and colleges use it too, for their own aid." Her mother clicked through to a state page and found the deadline there, weeks closer than either of them had assumed, and her hand went still on the mouse.

"Why didn't I know this," her mother said, not as a question. Mia was already digging the tax folder out of the drawer where the important papers lived in a rubber-banded stack. The two of them worked through the fields together, her mother reading numbers, Mia typing, the affective weight of each figure settling differently on each of them: her mother saw years of them, Mia saw only boxes that had to be filled correctly. They argued once, about whether to count the side income, and looked it up, and were wrong, and fixed it. At some point near one in the morning, Mia realized she had stopped thinking about whether she would get in. There was too much to do for the life that came after.

They submitted it. The confirmation number appeared, long and meaningless and somehow beautiful, and her mother sat back and pressed both palms to her eyes. "Now we wait on two things," she said.

In the kitchen's after-silence, with the laptop fan ticking down, Mia understood something she could not yet say cleanly. She had spent months treating the college's decision as the only verdict in town, delivered by some distant magistrate over whom she had no influence. But tonight the two of them had filed a claim of their own, a form that said, in effect, here is what we have, here is what we need, and it would go out into the same bureaucracy and be weighed. She could want this place and prepare for it and still not know. Both of those things could be true in the same body, the same late hour. What stayed uncertain was whether wanting something and preparing for it was hope or just a better organized kind of fear.

Her mother closed the laptop. "Go to sleep," she said. "You have school."

On the stairs, Mia's phone buzzed once in her pocket. She stood at the landing with her thumb over the screen, the kitchen light still warm behind her, and looked at it for a long moment before she opened the message.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Behavioral interview questions, such as 'Tell me about a time when...', are built on the idea that past behavior is a good predictor of future behavior.
story:
Blake had exactly one suit jacket, and it smelled like his grandfather's cedar closet, which was either an advantage or a problem depending on whether the manager at Hendricks Grocery appreciated subtlety. He stood in the kitchen of his grandparents' house, buttoning and unbuttoning the jacket while his grandmother dried a colander and pretended not to watch.

"Sit," she said finally, pointing the colander at a chair. "You're pacing like your grandfather before a colonoscopy."

The interview was Thursday. Blake had never had a job, had never been interviewed for anything, and had filled out the application in the parking lot of the library so his mother wouldn't hover. He wanted the job for reasons he could enumerate: money, the fall tuition deposit, something to put on a form next year that wasn't blank. But when he imagined Thursday, what he imagined was his own voice coming out thin and apologetic, and some man in a polo shirt writing one word on a pad.

Jaycee arrived at four, carrying her backpack and, inexplicably, a clipboard. "I googled," she announced. "I am now the most qualified interviewer in this county." She set the clipboard on the kitchen table, smoothed her invented paperwork, and became, visibly, someone else. "Blake. Thanks for coming in."

"Tell me about yourself," Blake began, before she could.

"That's my line, but fine, go." She scribbled something that was certainly a doodle.

He talked for ninety seconds about being a senior, reliable, good with people, and heard every sentence sag at the end like a tent in rain. Jaycee let him finish, then flipped the clipboard over. It was blank.

"Okay, here's the thing. The real questions aren't about yourself. They're like, tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult customer. Tell me about a time you failed." She tapped the pen against her teeth. "They're called behavioral interview questions. The whole idea is that past behavior predicts future behavior. So they don't care what you would do. They care what you did."

"So I need stories."

"You need receipts."

Blake slumped, and that was when his grandfather wandered in from the garage with an ebullient expression that meant he'd either fixed the lawnmower or broken it in an interesting way. He was carrying two bottles of root beer, which he distributed like medals, and he settled into the chair across from Blake with the authority of a man who had hired perhaps four people in his life and remembered all of them.

"Practice on me," he said. "I've been interviewed. In 1961 a man asked me if I could lift a hundred-pound sack of flour, and I said yes, and I could not."

"Tell me about a time you worked as part of a team," Jaycee read, or pretended to read, from the blank clipboard.

Blake opened his mouth and found the cupboard bare. No customers, no shifts, no workplace anything. Jaycee interposed before the silence could calcify. "It doesn't have to be a job, genius. That's the trick. School counts. Use the physics boat thing."

The physics boat thing was a project from junior year: four students, one balsa wood boat, a weight requirement, and Jersey, who had insisted on a hull design everyone else doubted and who turned out to be right, though the boat still sank on its second run. Blake started telling it and it came out flat, a list of events. His grandfather shook his head.

"You're giving a report," he said. "Tell it like the boat mattered."

So Blake told it again, and this time he looked at his grandfather while he did it, because that was the other thing Jaycee had printed out, that eye contact thing, and something shifted. The story had a shape. A conflict, a decision, a failure that taught the group to test earlier. When he finished, the failure part landed almost like a strength, and Jaycee pointed the pen at him and said, "See? Sinking boat, non-sinking answer."

His grandmother, who had been quietly shelling peas at the counter this whole time, spoke without turning around. "You know the boy who bagged groceries there when I did my shopping on Saturdays. Loud boy. Very cheerful." She dropped a handful of pods into the bowl. "They kept him. He gave every customer a joke, whether they wanted it or not. Some of them did not."

"That's an externality," Blake said. "Costs imposed on bystanders. We just covered it in econ."

"His jokes were a public good," his grandfather countered. "You can't fence off a joke."

They argued about this through the rest of the peas, and Blake, listening, understood something small but real: the cheerful bagger and the sinking boat were the same kind of evidence. What you had already done was what they would believe about you, and the best he could offer was a flawed project and a grandparent's kitchen. It wasn't certainty. It was a considered bet on himself, made with the materials available. He rehearsed the boat story twice more, once for Jaycee and once for the bathroom mirror, where he practiced not blinking like a startled deer.

Thursday came. The manager, a tired woman named only by the tag on her chest, slid a sheet of questions across the desk and said, "Tell me about a time you had to learn something quickly."

Blake leaned forward, held her eyes, and began, "There's this boat I have to tell you about." She wrote something down. It looked like it might be a check mark. It was not. It was the letter of the day the orientation was, which conflicted with his physics final, and when he asked whether he could do the other orientation date, she said, "Tell me about a time you handled a scheduling conflict." Blake laughed. "I'm not going to tell you about the boat again," he said. "You were there."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Many food banks cannot accept home-cooked or opened food, because they cannot check how it was prepared or stored.
story:
Hayden arrived at the community garden at nine with a signed waiver in his backpack and no idea what to do with his hands. Ms. Addo met him at the gate, pointing him toward the folding tables set up beside the tomato beds, where three volunteers were sorting boxes of donated cans into rows. One of them, a girl from his chemistry class named Mariam, waved him over and handed him a clipboard. "You're on intake," she said. "Weigh it, log it, shelve it. It's not hard, but it has rules, and the rules matter more than you'd think."

The garden had been a vacant lot until two springs ago, when the church on one side of the street and the mosque on the other agreed to share it, and Mariam told him that the founding families had been proud of that, proud that nothing about the place had ever turned sectarian, that the plots were mixed and the water bill was split and the arguments were only about compost. The food bank operated out of the same lot on Saturday mornings, under a canopy with a green tarp that had begun to peel at one corner, its cheerful paint a thin veneer over older, rustier frames. Hayden took his place at the intake table and waited for the donations to come.

They came steadily at first. A man dropped off two grocery bags of canned beans. A woman brought a case of pasta, still sealed, still well within its date. Hayden weighed everything on the hanging scale, and when the numbers came in messy, fractions he couldn't read cleanly, he learned to interpolate between the marks, reading the needle between two and two and a half pounds and writing down his best estimate. Ms. Addo checked his sheet once, nodded, and moved on to help an elderly volunteer carry a crate. The morning had a rhythm to it, and Hayden started to feel useful in the specific way that makes a Saturday morning feel earned.

Then a neighbor arrived, a small woman he didn't know, holding a foil pan with a dish towel folded over it like a gift. Steam still rose faintly from under the foil. "It's lasagna," she said. "I made it this morning. For the food bank. My mother always did this, back home, when someone was in trouble." She set it on his table with both hands, gently, and stepped back as though she had entrusted him with something alive.

Hayden looked at the lasagna and then at his clipboard, which had a laminated sheet taped to the back, a list of what could be accepted and what could not. Sealed, commercially packaged food, yes. Fresh produce from the garden, yes. But home-cooked food, food whose lids had been broken, food that had been opened, no. He read it twice, hoping it would rearrange itself. It didn't. He understood, slowly, that it wasn't about her cooking, which he was sure was better than anything on the shelves behind him. It was that once a container was opened or made in someone's kitchen, nobody at the food bank could know how it had been prepared or stored, and so they couldn't take it, couldn't check it, couldn't pass it on to anyone who was hungry.

"I'm so sorry," he said. "We can't accept it. Not because of you. It's the rule for everybody's homemade food." He felt the words come out clumsy, and he tried again, softer. "I can't verify how it was kept, so I'm not allowed to take it, even though I'm sure it's wonderful." The woman looked at the pan, then at the rows of cans, dented and labeled and anonymous, and something in her face closed. "Cans," she said. "Fine. It's fine." She picked up the pan and turned to go.

"Wait," Hayden said, before he had decided to say anything. There was a bench near the fence where the sorting volunteers took their breaks, and the crates were heavy, and the morning was long. "Would you stay and share it with us? With me, I mean. If it's already made, and it's here." He knew, even as he said it, that he was working around the rule rather than with it, that he was guessing rather than knowing whether this was allowed. But she paused, and Ms. Addo, who had been listening from the tomato beds, gave a small shrug that Hayden chose to read as permission.

Mariam brought paper plates. Another volunteer, Madelyn, whom Hayden vaguely remembered from a middle school orchestra concert, found forks in the supply box, and the five of them sat on the bench in the sun and ate the lasagna, which was, as he had suspected, better than anything on the shelves. The woman's name, he learned, was not offered, so he didn't press for it; she watched them eat and said her mother would have liked seeing this. Hayden went back to the intake table with the taste of it still in his mouth and a question he couldn't settle: whether the rule was a kindness or a failure of trust, whether the same system that kept people safe also kept them at a distance, whether the lasagna had been wasted or honored by what they'd done. He weighed the next bag of beans, read the needle between two marks, and wrote down his best guess. Madelyn slid another crate toward him and said, "Table four, and then we break for lunch."

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937, and Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it.
story:
The pond behind the school had frozen in patches, each one a different thickness, and Jade chose the widest to lay her notes on, pinning them with a rock so the wind couldn't take them. Serena sat cross-legged on the dock in her coat, boots off, socks stretched toward the sun as if that could warm them. Annalise stood at the edge reading the study guide upside down, which was how she claimed she learned best, though her quiz averages did not augur well for the method.

"Okay," Jade said. "Glucose goes in. Then what."

"Then magic," Annalise said. "Then ATP comes out and everyone's happy."

"That's not an answer, that's a prayer."

The exam was Monday. Mr. Yang had told them, on the way out of the last class, that half of them would fail the respiration diagram, that every year half of them did, in a tone that was neither cruel nor kind, just factual, like weather. Jade had decided over the weekend that she would not be in that half, and had also decided, less nobly, that she would drag Serena and Annalise with her, whether they wanted to be dragged or not.

"Pyruvate," Serena said, eyes closed, face turned up. "Glucose splits. Pyruvate. Then it gets into the mitochondria and then, the cycle."

"Which cycle?"

"The circular one."

Jade flipped the page. The diagram on it was drawn like a wheel with carbons riding the rim, citrate at the top, and beside it in the textbook's margin, in small print, Krebs cycle. She had read the phrase a hundred times without seeing it. "Why does it have a guy's name on it? Krebs. Who's Krebs?"

"Probably the one who won something," Annalise said. She got out her phone, thumbs working, and Jade watched her face change from boredom to interest, which on Annalise was nearly an event. "Okay, so. Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937."

"Described it," Jade repeated. "Like they found it, not invented it."

"Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it."

"Shared," Serena said, eyes still closed. "Shared with who?"

Annalise scrolled. "Doesn't say yet. Some other guy."

"Johnson didn't get it?" Jade asked.

"Maybe he died," Serena said. "Maybe he was rude at conferences."

Jade laughed, and the laugh came out strange, because something had snagged in her. She thought of the diagram again, the wheel with its carbons turning, the thing that happened in every cell of every person at the pond, in the geese, in the frozen algae. Nobody had made it. Krebs had just watched it closely enough to write it down, and a committee in Stockholm had given him a medal, and now his name rode on the wheel like a brand. She wasn't sure whether that seemed wonderful to her or like an indictment of how credit gets handed out, one man's name for a process that belonged to everything alive, and to Johnson too, who was a footnote on Annalise's phone.

"Wait," Serena said, sitting up. "So the cycle isn't named after the cycle. It's named after the watcher."

"It's called both," Annalise said. "Citric acid cycle, Krebs cycle. Same thing."

"Okay," Jade said slowly. "So glucose splits, pyruvate crosses into the mitochondria, and then the citric acid cycle turns, and somewhere in all that the energy gets banked as ATP. Krebs didn't build the bank. He just read the ledger."

"That's a weird way to study," Serena said, but she wrote it down.

They worked the path in order, each of them holding one stage in memory, walking the dock like a procession: Jade was glycolysis, Annalise was pyruvate crossing the membrane, Serena was the cycle itself, spinning in place with her arms out. When one of them forgot a step, the others jeered, and a man fishing from the far bank looked over at the three girls circling and muttering about electrons, and packed up his tackle early.

"You know what I keep thinking," Jade said, when they had stopped for the sandwiches. The pond had gone amber at the edges, the ice softening into a sedimentary layer of old leaves pressed under new water. "Last year I quit biology after one bad test. I decided I wasn't a science person, like that was a fact about me. And now I'm out here and I actually want to get this right."

"You weren't a science person," Serena said, "or you didn't want to do the work?"

"I honestly don't know. Maybe both. Maybe the wanting came after."

Annalise lay back on the dock, phone on her chest. "For the record, I still think it's magic."

"It's not magic," Jade said. "It's a wheel with a man's name on it, turning whether he ever looked or not." She picked up the rock, released her pages, and the wind took two of them out over the ice, white squares skidding toward the dark water, and Serena was already running.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: For Mexico's Day of the Dead on November 1 and 2, families build home altars called ofrendas with orange marigolds, whose bright color and strong scent are believed to guide souls home.
story:
The invitation had a marigold on it, which Gabriel recognized before he recognized anything else, because his grandmother had pressed one into his grandfather's funeral program eleven months ago and he had kept it in his wallet like evidence of something he couldn't name. The cultural center was hosting a Day of the Dead celebration on the second of November, and his mother had decided, with the sudden authority she deployed for holidays, that the whole family was going, and that Gabriel was carrying the box.

The box contained his grandfather's photograph, a small loaf of pan dulce that his mother had baked at eleven at night, and a letter Gabriel had found in September, tucked into the back of his grandfather's tool chest. He had not opened it. Opening it felt like signing something, and he was eighteen, and he had opinions about signing things he hadn't read, though apparently not about carrying them across a parking lot.

At the center, Mr. Zhao, who ran the place and had once lent Gabriel a soldering iron with alarming generosity, met them at the door. "The community ofrenda is in the west room," he said. "You know the word? Ofrendas. Home altars. Families build them these two days, November first and second." Gabriel said he did know, sort of, from a documentary he'd half watched while doing calculus, and Mr. Zhao looked at him with the patience of a man who had heard worse confessions.

The west room smelled of cempasúchil, which Gabriel did not know was the word for marigold until a woman at the door said it, holding an armful of them like a bouquet of small suns. "Take some," she said. "The color and the smell, they say that's how the souls find their way back. The bright and the strong." She said it lightly, the way you'd explain a house rule. Gabriel took three and tried not to be weird about it, and was weird about it anyway, holding them stems-up like a person who had never been handed flowers in his life.

Riley was already there, standing near the altar with Jessa, who was photographing everything for a class project and narrating under her breath. "Okay so this family has seven candles and a guitar, that's confidence," Jessa said. "This one has a bowl of shrimp. Somebody's grandmother really liked shrimp." Riley, who was phlegmatic about most things including grief, which Gabriel both admired and resented, nodded at the photos. "My abuela's coming later," Riley said. "She wants to put my grandpa's watch on the altar. I told her the watch is a family heirloom and she told me so is he."

Gabriel laughed, and then felt the laugh snag on the box in his hands. He set his grandfather's photograph at the edge of the altar, between the shrimp family and the guitar family, and discovered that placing it felt less like a ceremony and more like setting a table, which he found he didn't mind. His mother behind him made a small sound, not quite a word. The marigolds went in front of the frame, orange and loud, and Gabriel caught their scent and understood, in a way no documentary had managed, why anyone would believe a smell could call somebody home. It smelled like the front hallway of his grandfather's house. It smelled like being nine.

"You look like you're doing math," Riley said.

"I'm doing philosophy," Gabriel said. "Which is worse." He explained, in a low voice so his mother wouldn't hear and be interested, that he had two versions of himself arguing. One said the dead don't travel, don't smell flowers, don't need a trail, and that the altar was a beautiful thing people did for themselves. The other said his grandfather had been so stubborn in life that death seemed unlikely to have improved his compliance, and if there was any chance a soul could be guided anywhere by orange petals, his grandfather would follow them out of sheer curiosity. "I can't get them to agree," Gabriel said. "I can't abrogate either of them. They both seem true."

"That's the worst deal I've ever heard," Riley said, but kindly.

Jessa, who had been eavesdropping with her whole body, pointed at his jacket. "Is that a letter? You've been holding it like it's going to bite." Gabriel admitted it was from the tool chest, and that he'd been keeping it sealed, and Riley said, "That's a whole year of postage for nothing," which made no sense and somehow made perfect sense. Gabriel stepped out to the hallway, because a letter deserved better than an audience, and opened it.

His grandfather's handwriting was the same terrible handwriting that had labeled every drawer in the garage. The letter was not a farewell, which Gabriel had been dreading. It was a list. A chronology, actually, of unfinished projects, dated and itemized: the birdhouse, the fence gate, the transistor radio Gabriel had been forbidden to open at age eleven and was now, in writing, formally authorized to open. The last line said, "When you come do these, put on the radio. It's boring working quiet." There was no date on the letter and no mention of dying, and Gabriel sat down on a hallway chair and held it and thought that his grandfather had written him not a goodbye but a to-do list, which was the most him thing possible, and that maybe that was what an ofrenda was too: not a goodbye, a to-do list. A thing you kept setting up so the unfinished could stay unfinished in company.

He went back in. His mother was straightening the photograph a quarter inch, an improvement no one could verify. Mr. Zhao was explaining the shrimp to a newcomer. Jessa had found a family whose ofrenda held a dog's collar and was quietly losing it in the corner. Gabriel took the marigolds he'd placed and rearranged them so the blooms faced the photo directly, because if scent was a path, he figured, you wanted the path pointed at the right house.

"Do you believe it?" Riley asked, coming to stand beside him. "The souls coming back."

"I believe the marigolds are doing something," Gabriel said. "I don't know what. I'm keeping both." He tapped his grandfather's picture. "We've got a radio to fix, apparently. You hold the screwdriver."

Riley said, "I've never held a screwdriver in my life," and Gabriel said, "Then this weekend you'll learn," and set the letter, finally, on the altar beside the pan dulce, where the marigolds could reach it.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says that if F is an antiderivative of f, then the integral of f from a to b equals F(b) minus F(a).
story:
The library smelled like toner and the lemon cleaner the custodian used on tables nobody touched, and Austin had spread forty-one torn notebook pages across the widest one, near the periodicals, where the lamps actually worked. Each page held rectangles. He was adding up the areas of rectangles under the curve of x squared, from zero to three, because the scholarship exam was Saturday and the practice test had a question worth more points than any other, and the only method he trusted was the one he'd taught himself from an old textbook in the back stacks: slice the region thin, multiply width by height, add everything. Four hundred rectangles gave him an answer near nine. Eight hundred gave him something nearer still. The answer was creeping toward nine like a cat toward a door, and he was running out of paper and, by his count, of days.

"You're doing it wrong," said Katarina, dropping her bag on the chair opposite him.

"I'm doing it the only way I know how."

"You look like a man trying to indemnify himself against the math. Like if you draw enough rectangles, the exam board can never sue you." She picked up a page, squinted at the columns of figures. "There's a formula, Austin. My cousin showed me last summer. Two lines. Done."

He said he didn't believe in two lines. He believed in work you could see, each rectangle honest and countable, and she rolled her eyes and went to find Judah, who was allegedly in the computer lab but who appeared twelve minutes later with a paper cup of vending-machine hot chocolate and the expression of someone with incipient wisdom and no desire to share it for free.

"Eight hundred rectangles," Judah said, whistling. "That's devotion. That's the opposite of efficiency, but it's devotion."

"Do you know the formula or not?"

Judah set down his cup. He drew the curve on a fresh page, smooth and quick. Then, at the bottom, he wrote two letters and a minus sign, and Austin leaned in, and the pace of everything slowed, because Judah's pencil had stopped and he was grinning in a way that meant a price was coming.

The price was Austin's parking spot for a week, which was a scandalous offer, since Austin didn't have a car and the spot was his mother's, transferred to him by the family's private modularity arrangement: she drove the car, he nominally owned the space, and on weekends he rented it to Judah's brother for ten dollars. Austin had been earning forty a month from a rectangle of asphalt. He thought about eight hundred rectangles of paper. He said fine.

Judah wrote it out. He said that if you had a function, and you found its antiderivative, called F, then the whole area under the curve came down to F at the end point minus F at the start point. Integral from a to b equals F of b minus F of a. He said it fast, the way people say things they don't want to be charged for explaining twice.

"So for x squared," Austin said slowly, "the antiderivative is x cubed over three."

"If you say so."

"From zero to three. Three cubed over three, minus zero cubed over three." He did it in the margin. "Nine. Exactly nine. No rectangles. No creep, no cat at the door."

The twist arrived when Ms. Nguyen came over to close the periodicals section, saw the torn pages, and asked why he hadn't used the note she'd left him. What note, Austin asked. The note, she said, folded into the practice test she'd handed back last Thursday, the one marked see reference shelf, 515 N, which had been sitting in his binder for five days, page down, under a permission slip and a receipt. She had written two lines on it and assumed he'd found them. He unbuckled his binder with hands that felt too large. There it was, in her small teacher handwriting: the same theorem, the same F of b minus F of a, sitting quietly beside the question it answered, the whole time, while he drew rectangle number six hundred and eleven.

"So you traded a parking spot," Katarina said, "for information that was already in your binder."

"I traded a parking spot," Austin said, "for information I actually read."

Judah raised his cup in something like respect. Austin gathered the torn pages, all forty-one, and walked them to the recycling bin by the window, feeding them in one at a time, watching each rectangle go.

"Four a month," Katarina called after him. "You're down to four a month, and your mother's going to hear about it."

"Let her hear," Austin said, and dropped in the last page.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: When muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue making 2 ATP per glucose.
story:
The mitochondria exhibit hummed behind glass, a wall of animated cells rendered in blue and gold, and Cameron stood in front of it with his worksheet half filled out. He had come to the museum because Mr. Reddy had offered extra credit to anyone who could trace cellular respiration from beginning to end without looking it up afterward, and Cameron needed the credit more than he wanted to admit. The test was Thursday. He had until the bus left at four.

"It's like a factory," Kylie said, appearing at his elbow with popcorn she wasn't supposed to have in the exhibit hall. "Glucose comes in, energy goes out. Done."

"That's not an answer, that's a slogan."

"Fine, genius, what's the answer?"

He didn't have one yet. That was the problem. He could recite the words, glycolysis, pyruvate, the Krebs cycle, the way he could recite song lyrics, and none of it connected to anything. The animation on the wall showed a glucose molecule splitting, and small glowing coins of ATP popping loose, and Cameron copied the sequence onto his worksheet and felt nothing click.

Natalie arrived ten minutes later, out of breath, her jacket tied around her waist. "Missed the bus at school. Ran the last two blocks."

"Your legs burning?" Kylie asked.

"Obviously."

Cameron looked up from the worksheet. Something Natalie had said in class last week surfaced, something about her track season, about the 400 meters, about how the last hundred felt like running through water. "When you sprint," he said slowly, "your cells run out of oxygen."

"That's why I do intervals, yes."

"And there's this stuff. Pyruvate." He tapped the glass where the animation had moved on to the mitochondrion, its folded inner membrane lit like a canyon. "When your muscle cells run low on oxygen, they turn pyruvate into lactate. That's the word. Lactate."

"Lactic acid," Natalie said. "My coach vilifies it. Blames it for everything, soreness, slow times, the weather probably."

"And that's the part that's wrong," Cameron said, and even as he said it he wasn't sure how he knew, only that the diagram was pulling him toward it. The animation had cycled back to the cell's cytoplasm, and there was a second, smaller loop he'd ignored the first time through. Glucose splitting, pyruvate forming, pyruvate becoming lactate, and something else returning to the start of the loop. He leaned in. The returning something was labeled NAD+.

"So it's not the villain?"

"Look at the loop." He traced it on the glass. "Lactate gets made, and that regenerates NAD+, so glycolysis can keep going. It's not sabotage. It's the cell keeping the lights on the only way it can." The caption beneath the loop, when he found it, confirmed the arithmetic: 2 ATP per glucose. Not the thirty-odd the full mitochondrial process yielded, but two more than zero. "When your legs are dying at the end of a race, that's your cells scraping together two ATP at a time instead of quitting."

Natalie folded her arms and studied the loop for a long moment. "So my coach has been lecturing us about the enemy and it's actually the rescue crew."

"Basically."

Mr. Reddy found them there fifteen minutes later, doing his rounds with a lanyard and a cup of coffee, and read over Cameron's shoulder in silence. "You've got the whole chain down," he said. "Most students stop at the mitochondrion and treat the anaerobic part as a footnote."

"It's not a footnote if it's what's happening every time somebody sprints," Cameron said.

"That's a fair epistemology for a Tuesday afternoon." Mr. Reddy drained his coffee. "But be careful which sources you trust. There's an older textbook in the gift shop that still gets the lactate story wrong, because the error was endemic for decades. Everybody repeated it because everybody else had. The question is always how you know what you know." He walked on toward the physics floor before Cameron could decide whether that had been praise or a warning.

Cameron sat down on the bench across from the exhibit and looked at his worksheet. The sequence was all there now, glucose to pyruvate to the mitochondria's long harvest, with the lactate loop drawn at the margin like a side road that turned out to be the road you actually drove on during a hard sprint. He believed it. He also knew that what he believed had come from a museum animation and a caption and a phrase of Mr. Reddy's, that he hadn't run the experiments, hadn't read the papers, that two weeks ago he would have agreed with the coach about lactic acid without a second thought. He wrote a question mark next to the loop and decided he'd leave it there.

"Bus in five," Kylie said, balling up her popcorn bag.

Natalie pulled her jacket loose and shook out her arms like she was at a starting line. "Two ATP per glucose," she said. "I'm going to say that to my coach at practice tomorrow and watch his face."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: An adjustable-rate mortgage's interest rate changes periodically with a market index, so its monthly payment can rise, unlike a fixed-rate mortgage's.
story:
Violet had walked past the real estate office on Alder Street a hundred times without going in, but today the flyer in the window stopped her: one bedroom, newly listed, and the price printed in a bold red number that was almost, if she squinted, within reach. Her mother had said it out loud only once, over dishes, that the landlord was selling their building and they had until spring. Violet had said nothing, then went to her room and started a notebook with columns in it.

Inside, the office smelled of coffee and warm paper. A man at the front desk, his nameplate reading Mr. González, looked up from a file. "Help you?" The question was not unkind, though he studied her school backpack as if trying to place her.

"I saw the one bedroom," Violet said. "In the window. Can I ask what happens after the rent part? Like, is there more?" She felt her ears go hot, but she kept her voice level, the way she did when asking a lab partner to repeat a measurement she'd missed.

Mr. González turned the monitor toward her and walked her through it line by line. Rent each month, and before that a security deposit, roughly a month's rent, held against damage and returned when she left if the place was kept decent. "And if you were buying instead," he added, tapping a different screen, "you'd save for a down payment, a fraction of the price up front, and a bank lends you the rest." She copied it all in her notebook, her handwriting going smaller as the numbers grew. It occurred to her that a building could be a machine with all these gears, and that nobody had ever shown her the gears.

Behind her, a woman at the second desk was arguing quietly on the phone. "Nothing changed, that's what I keep telling you. Same house, same bank, same everything, and the payment went up by three hundred dollars this year." She caught Violet listening and lowered her voice, but not before Violet heard, "No, the rate does that, it's an adjustable-rate mortgage, the payment can go up." When the woman hung up, she pressed her fingers to her temples like someone holding a door shut.

"Excuse me," Violet said, before she could decide not to. "Did you say the payment changed even though nothing else did? How can that be true?" The woman, Ms. someone, gave a tired almost-smile. "Adjustable-rate," she said again, slower this time, as if Violet were her nephew. "The rate moves with the market. My sister's fixed-rate never moves. That's the trade." Violet wrote fixed on one side of a line and adjustable on the other, and felt the two words sit there like opposing results from the same experiment, the kind her immunology unit called different responses to the same stimulus. Her father had been phlegmatic about their own housing talk, shrugging at the kitchen table, but she had never been able to shrug at anything she didn't understand.

She sat with Mr. González a while longer while he helped another couple at the far desk, and she filled the margins of her page. If she could save the deposit by June, and her mother's hours held steady, the one bedroom was possible, though possible was a wide word, wide enough to hide things in. Buying, with the down payment, was somewhere past the horizon of her notebook. And now there was this new fact, that even people who owned could watch their numbers move under them. She caught herself wondering whether the woman on the phone had known, when she signed, what she was agreeing to, or whether anyone fully knows.

Outside, she texted Emmitt: did his parents rent or own, and did he know which kind of mortgage, fixed or the other one? He replied with a shrugging emoji and "no idea, why," and Noor, added to the thread, wrote "my dad talks about refinance at dinner, it's like a whole religion." Violet smiled at the sidewalk. She didn't have an answer yet, only a sharper set of questions, and a notebook whose last line read, in her smallest handwriting, "same house, different payments."

She walked home the long way, past the building with the red flyer reflected in its lobby glass, and stopped on the corner to reread her columns. Then she closed the notebook, slid the rubber band around it twice, and crossed the street toward the door where her mother's plants stood in the window.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Monet showed fifteen paintings from his Haystacks series at the Durand-Ruel gallery in May 1891, and most sold within a month.
story:
