Jordyn had spread her grandmother's watercolors across the kitchen table, twenty of them, all of the same stretch of river behind the house. Her grandmother had painted the bend from the porch for forty years, morning and evening, summer and the grey weeks of March. Now the table was covered with water and light, and Jordyn's own sketchbook lay open at a page with one word on it: theme.

"You're doing this here?" her grandmother said, setting down two mugs. "In my kitchen?"

"The deadline's Monday. Ten pieces, one theme, plus a statement." Jordyn turned one of the watercolors toward the window. "I keep thinking ten pictures of one thing is lazy. Like I couldn't think of anything else."

Her grandmother pulled out a chair but didn't sit. "When I was in school they'd have called it obsession. A whole term on one bend of river. They'd have wanted an explanation."

"That's the artist's statement." Jordyn pulled her laptop toward her and opened the blank document, which had a title and then nothing, the cursor blinking in the white like something trapped. "I've written it four times and deleted it four times. It keeps coming out prolix, all these sentences trying to justify myself, and I don't even believe them." She closed the laptop again.

That afternoon Ibraheem cycled over, helmet still on, holding his phone like a dispatch. "Brianne says you think repetition is cheating," he said. "So I looked it up. Monet showed fifteen paintings from his Haystacks series at the Durand-Ruel gallery in May 1891, and most sold within a month." He dropped into the chair across from her and pulled off the helmet. "Fifteen haystacks. Same field, same stacks. People lined up to buy them."

Jordyn looked past him at the watercolors. She had been treating the theme like a debt she owed, something to be excused, and here was this fact sitting on the table between the mugs like an acquittal. Not her own, exactly; Monet hadn't been thinking of her. But if fifteen paintings of haystacks could hang in one gallery and sell, then ten drawings of a river bend weren't a confession of poverty. They were an argument. Still, the word "most" snagged in her mind; not all of them sold, and she didn't know what the buyers saw, whether they wanted one haystack or the whole weather of them. She held that question instead of answering it.

"Show me what you've got," Ibraheem said, so she did: four drawings of the river already finished, done at different hours, and the sketchbook with notes on six more. He leaned over each one without touching it, which she appreciated. "This one's the best," he said, pointing at the evening drawing where the water had gone the color of the underside of a leaf.

"That's the one I almost threw out. I thought it was too dark." She turned it so they could both see. From next door, Ms. Pritchard's mower started up, and then stopped, and started again, patient as a second clock.

Jordyn worked until the light went, and after supper she opened the laptop once more. This time she wrote three sentences and stopped, because three was all she meant: that she had drawn one river ten times because it was never the same river twice, and that she wasn't sure yet whether she was documenting the water or her own looking, and that the not-knowing was part of the work. It wasn't an explanation. It was more like a doorway she was willing to stand in. She saved it, carried the evening drawing to the porch rail, and propped it facing the real bend of water, where the last light was going off it like a lamp being carried into another room.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Near the edges of real plates the field lines bulge outward and the field weakens, an effect called fringing, so E = V/d holds best near the centre.
story:
"Forty-one volts per centimetre," Anas read off the multimeter, and Jonathan wrote it down even though it was wrong.

Their exhibit sat at the end of the third row, two aluminium plates bolted to a wooden frame twelve centimetres apart, a power supply humming under the table. Jonathan had spent six weeks on it. The plan had been simple: hold the voltage steady at sixty volts, slide a probe along the centre line, and show the judges that the field strength stayed flat at five volts per centimetre everywhere, exactly as E = V/d predicted. A graph like a tabletop. Proof that the formula was real and not just something Ms. Luo had written on the board in October.

Bently crouched by the frame, threading the probe between the plates. "Move it toward the middle."

"Try the left side first," Jonathan said. "The side that failed."

Anas eased the probe along its track until it sat two centimetres from the left edge of the plates. The meter settled. Thirty-one volts per centimetre. Then twenty-six. At the very edge it wavered like something nervous.

"That's not a rounding error," Anas said.

"It's a wiring problem." Jonathan was already under the table, checking leads, wiggling connectors. The meter did not care. He climbed back up, wiped his palms on his trousers, and found Ms. Luo standing at the aisle with a clipboard and the expression she wore when she wanted you to talk first.

"Show me your data," she said.

Jonathan turned his notebook around. The centre measurements hugged the line at five volts per centimetre, beautiful, obedient. The outer ones fell away in a long sagging curve.

"Your wiring is fine," she said. "I watched you check it twice."

"Then the formula's wrong somewhere, or I built it wrong."

"Or," said Bently, from the floor, "the formula only works where you think it does." He said it lightly, the way he said most things, and Jonathan almost dismissed it. But he looked again at the curve, at the way it dropped precisely where the probe left the centre and wandered toward the plate edges, and something rearranged itself in his head. He had been treating the plates as if they extended forever in every direction, infinite sheets in an infinite universe, and his real plates were twelve by twenty centimetres of aluminium on a wooden frame.

"Ms. Luo," he said, "is there a name for this?"

She wrote something on her clipboard. "There is. But you're going to find it before the judges come by in forty minutes, because they'll ask, and 'my data looks bad near the edges' is not an answer." She moved on down the row.

They had no laptops allowed on the floor, so Anas held his phone while Jonathan scrolled, his thumb moving faster than his judgment. Half the internet wanted to sell them a textbook. Bently read over his shoulder and kept saying "no, no, no" to pages Jonathan had already stopped reading.

"There," Anas said. "Look at the diagram."

The page showed two plates and their field lines drawn between them, and near the centre the lines ran straight and parallel, like tram rails. At the edges the lines bowed outward, bulging past the plates as if escaping. Near the edges of real plates, the caption said, the field lines bulge outward and the field weakens. There was a word for it, printed in bold at the start of the paragraph.

"Fringing," Jonathan said. He said it twice, the second time quieter. He looked up at Anas. "So E = V/d holds best near the centre. It's not wrong. It's a promise with a boundary on it."

"Which you didn't know you'd made," Anas said.

At home Jonathan's father called this kind of thing rationalism, the faith that a tidy equation could hold the whole world, and he said it like a compliment and a warning at the same time. Jonathan had always thought the warning part was for other people. He copied the diagram into his notebook, freehand, plate edges and bulging lines, and drew his own measurement points on top. Every sagging point sat where a line curved.

"Judges," Bently said. "Two minutes. Row three."

The first judge was a man with a lanyard and tired eyes. He looked at the original graph, the clean flat line, and then at the notebook page where Jonathan had taped the new curve. "Why did you keep both?"

"Because the first one is what I hoped for," Jonathan said, "and the second one is what happened. The field is weaker near the edges of the plates because the field lines bulge outward there. Fringing. It means my numbers aren't broken."

The judge leaned closer to the frame, where the probe still hung near the left plate, its reading steady and low, almost malevolent in its patience. He tapped the meter's glass with one finger.

"So show me," he said. "Slide it."

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: The last time a British monarch refused royal assent to a bill was in 1708, when Queen Anne vetoed the Scottish Militia Bill.
story:
The folding chairs in the town hall gym were arranged in a horseshoe, and Alexis took the seat marked for the sponsor of Bill C-3, the weekend bus service petition she had been drafting since October. She had written it twice, once as a rant and once as a bill, and Ms. Fortin had circled the operative clause and written "this is the part that becomes law" in green ink. The first draft had said the town should be less awful to teenagers without cars. The second said that the transit authority shall operate Route 4 on Saturdays between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. Ms. Fortin had called that progress. "You've found a way to operationalize the complaint," she said, and Alexis had written the verb down because she suspected it would be useful.

Anissa was clerking, at the table with the binder and the stopwatch, because she wanted the procedural jobs, the ones where you decided what was allowed to happen next. Colton sat across the horseshoe as an opposition member. He had come to the meeting with a spreadsheet showing Saturday ridership projections from three comparable towns, and he wanted, Alexis was fairly sure, to be the person who found the flaw nobody else had found.

The bill went to committee first. That was the part Alexis had not expected to matter. Three students took it apart clause by clause while the public rows watched: whether "shall" meant mandatory, whether the fare should be stated, who would pay the driver. An old man from the third row, an actual ratepayer who came to all the real council meetings, raised his hand and asked whether the bill had considered insurance. It had not. Anissa wrote an amendment on a slip of paper and slid it across the table, and the committee adopted it in ninety seconds, and Alexis watched her careful second draft become a third document she had not entirely written. She noted that down too. A bill, it turned out, was less like an essay than like a fence that everyone added rails to.

In debate, Colton stood. He said his spreadsheet showed Saturday service running at a loss in two of his three comparison towns, and that the third had a university. Alexis had a rebuttal prepared, about extrinsic benefits, things outside the spreadsheet: shifts at the grocery store, the library, the arena, visits to the hospital an hour away. She said the loss per rider was not the same as the loss per town. Colton said that was a value judgment dressed as arithmetic, and she said so was his, and the Speaker, a senior named to no role anyone remembered assigning her, called the exchange repetitious and moved to the vote.

The vote came after lunch. Alexis counted hands while Anissa counted hands, and they matched: 31 to 29 in favour, on division. Anissa read the numbers into the record, and Alexis felt the horseshoe go quiet in a way she had not felt during any part of the drafting. Then Ms. Fortin, who had drawn the monarch's role by lot that morning and wore a paper crown someone had made in art class, stood and said she was inclined to refuse the bill royal assent. She said it mildly, looking at the binder, but the room reacted as though a fire alarm had gone off. A boy in the second row said she could not just do that, and someone else said of course she could, she was the Queen, and the old ratepayer said that in his day the lieutenant governor signed whatever was put in front of him.

Alexis had her phone out under the table, because she had learned the hard way that her instincts about what was realistic were not themselves evidence. She searched the refusal of royal assent and found the number before she found the sentence: 1708. Queen Anne, the Scottish Militia Bill. The last time a British monarch refused royal assent to a bill was in 1708, when Queen Anne vetoed the Scottish Militia Bill. She read it twice and stood.

"The last time a monarch actually refused assent was 1708," she said. "Queen Anne, the Scottish Militia Bill. That's over three hundred years of signing everything." Ms. Fortin tilted the paper crown and said that the power still existed on paper, and Alexis said so did the power to declare war, and nobody was planning that either. Colton stood, on her side for the first time all day, and said that a ceremonial veto would wreck the verisimilitude of the simulation, which was the whole reason they were doing it in a real town hall with a real ratepayer in row three. The Speaker asked Ms. Fortin for her decision.

Ms. Fortin took off the crown, folded it once, and set it on the table beside the binder. "Royal assent is given," she said, and Anissa wrote the time in the record, 3:42, and underlined it twice. The old man in row three put on his coat and paused at the horseshoe's gap on his way out. "Next time put the insurance clause in before committee," he said. "It's your bill, not theirs." Alexis copied the words into the margin of her first draft.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The phrase 'rule of thirds' was first written down by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book Remarks on Rural Scenery.
story:
Joseph had been staring at the same stretch of canvas for twenty minutes when Cale leaned over his shoulder and said, "Your horizon is dead center. That's a crime against nature."

"It's a landscape," Joseph said. "Landscapes have horizons. Horizons go in the middle. That's where the world puts them."

The art classroom smelled of turpentine and the burnt-sugar snack bars Mr. Sun kept in the supply cabinet and sold at a markup nobody protested. Fourth period had dissolved into open studio time, which meant Mr. Sun sat at his desk grading with theatrical slowness while the eleven of them worked on pieces for the spring show. Joseph's piece was supposed to be the marsh behind his grandmother's house, the one with the crooked dock and the herons that stood so still you could mistake them for lawn ornaments. So far he had a lot of gray.

"Move it," Cale said. He picked up Joseph's brush, which Joseph had not offered him, and gestured at the canvas. "A third of the way down. Trust me. Rule of thirds."

"Who made that rule?"

Cale shrugged. "Art people. Dead guys, probably."

At the next table Harry was cutting mat board with a razor and a ruler, and she called over without looking up. "It's not a rule, it's a suggestion. My mom says composition teachers treat it like scripture, and half of them can't tell you where it came from."

Joseph looked at his horizon, sitting fat and unrepentant in the middle of the canvas, and felt the specific irritation of being told his instinct was wrong by people who also could not say why. He was not against rules. He was against rules that arrived without paperwork. "Somebody had to write it down first," he said. "Rules don't just float around in the air."

That night he sat at the kitchen table with his mother's old laptop, its fan wheezing like it resented being asked to do anything, and typed "who invented rule of thirds." He expected a fog of forums, the internet's usual habit of answering a question with six worse questions. Instead the answer came up clean: the phrase was first written down by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book, Remarks on Rural Scenery. Joseph read it twice. A real man, a real year, a real book with a title that sounded like something you'd find warped on a shelf in a summer house. For some reason this settled him. The rule had a birthday. It had an author. It was a decision someone made, not a law of physics, which meant it could be argued with.

He still moved the horizon. He spent Thursday after school repainting the sky, dragging the marsh line down until it sat a third of the way from the bottom, and he had to admit, grudgingly, that the canvas breathed differently afterward. The sky got taller. The water got more important. The heron he'd sketched near the dock now stood at a point where the eye wanted to land, which felt less like magic than like being handed a trick that had been working on him his whole life without his knowledge.

But the dock was still in the middle, and the dock was the thing he actually cared about. The dock was where his grandmother had taught him to bait a hook and where, last March, he had sat with his back against the post while the family divided up her belongings inside the house. He had listened through the window while they tried not to argue, and what he remembered most was not the marsh but the dock's specific loneliness, standing in the water apart from everything.

"It's the center that's gratuitous now," Harry said on Friday, walking past his easel with a cup of brush water she was definitely going to spill. "The composition thing, I mean. Cramming the interesting part off to the side just because a dead guy said skies like being tall."

"You read something?"

"You told me the dead guy's name. I looked him up. John Thomas Smith, 1797, Remarks on Rural Scenery. First person to write the phrase down." She set the cup down, successfully, on the counter. "But he wrote it down. He didn't invent seeing. People's eyes worked before 1797."

Joseph turned that over while he painted. He had spent the week thinking of Smith as an authority, then as a fraud, then, less dramatically, as a man who had noticed something and given it a name, the way you'd name a bird you'd seen a thousand times. The name was not the bird. Harry was right that people had balanced pictures forever, and Cale was right that the third-way-down genuinely looked better, and both of those things could be true without either of them canceling the other. He did not have to dichotomize it into rules versus freedom, though part of him wanted to, because picking a side was faster and felt more like having an opinion.

On Monday he made a decision that Mr. Sun noticed from across the room, because Mr. Sun noticed everything while appearing to notice nothing. Joseph kept the horizon at the third, low and horizontal, calm. But he centered the dock anyway, dead middle, vertical and dark against all that open water, breaking the rule on purpose because the painting was not about balance. It was about one thing standing alone, and every compositional trick he knew argued against doing that, which was exactly why he did it.

Mr. Sun came over during the last ten minutes, stood behind Joseph with his hands in his pockets, and looked for a long time. "You know that fights the whole composition," he said finally.

"I know," Joseph said.

"Good," said Mr. Sun, and pulled a snack bar out of his jacket, and set it on the edge of the easel like a wager on a horse he liked.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In US college admissions, a college's yield is the percentage of students it admits who then accept the offer and enroll.
story:
Savannah had arranged the kitchen table like a general arranging a battlefield, though the army consisted of one laptop, four brochures, a highlighter gone dry, and a mug of tea she kept forgetting to drink. The early decision answer from Calloway was due at five o'clock, and it was currently two.

"You've refreshed the portal six times," said Kelly, who had come over supposedly to study for chemistry but had migrated to the table with a bag of chips. "It's not going to change the answer by refreshing."

"I'm checking the time."

"There's a clock on the stove. It's right behind you. It's been right behind you your whole life."

Savannah closed the laptop with exaggerated dignity and pulled a brochure toward her instead. Calloway's cover photo showed students on a lawn, laughing at something off-camera, the kind of laughter that suggested they had never once refreshed anything. Below the photo, a line of small print bragged about the entering class. She read it twice. "It says the class of first-years is 'exceptionally committed.' What does that even mean? Committed to what?"

Kelly leaned over, crunching. "Committed to showing up, probably. My cousin did the tour there last spring. The guide kept going on about their yield. How it's, like, the highest in the region."

"Their what?"

"Yield. It's the percentage of students they admit who then accept the offer and enroll."

"That's a thing they measure?"

"Apparently it's a whole thing they brag about." Kelly tipped the bag and captured the last chips. "The guide was very proud. Some senior on the tour asked what it meant, and the guide got this glow, like a person being asked about their sourdough starter."

Savannah sat with that. The tea had gone cold, which was a small tragedy, but the idea warmed her anyway. She turned it over the way she turned over a chemistry problem, looking for the angle. "So when the brochure says the class is exceptionally committed, it means a lot of people who got in said yes."

"That would be the yield talking, yes."

"Which means..." Savannah pulled the laptop back open, not to refresh the portal this time but to look at her own list, the ordinary-decision applications she had half-finished in a drawer of the table, literal and metaphorical. "If I get in early, I have to go. That's the deal. And if I don't get in, I apply to the others, and if one of them takes me, I become a tiny percentage point in somebody's yield." She found this faintly hilarious. "I'm either a statistic they're proud of or a statistic they never count."

"You could also be a statistic they're sad about," Kelly offered. "A yield they lost. You could be their regret."

"Nobody at a college regrets me, Kelly."

"Impugning yourself is still impugning somebody. It's just inefficient."

Savannah laughed despite herself, and the laugh loosened something. For weeks the waiting had felt like a verdict on her entire person, on whether she was the sort of girl lawns are photographed for. But the yield made it stranger and smaller than that. The college wanted people to say yes; that was the game it was playing, with its brochures and its guides glowing like sourdough enthusiasts. Her wanting and its wanting were two separate engines, pointed at the same moment from opposite directions.

Bruce texted at three-fifteen: did u get in yet or r u being disaffected about it. She typed back that the word did not mean what he thought it meant, and he replied that it meant sad at a distance, which, she had to admit, was not the worst definition of waiting she'd heard. She set the phone face-down.

The specific thing she had not told anyone, not even Kelly, was that she had started to hope she didn't get in. Not really hoped. But there was a version of the next four years, at a school forty minutes from home with a co-op program and Bruce and Kelly nearby, that she had been sketching in the margins of her homework, and the early decision application sat on top of it like a rock on a drawing. She had applied to Calloway because it was the kind of school people nodded at, and she had never once interrogated the nod.

She interrogated it now, at the kitchen table, while her mother drifted through to wash grapes and offer them wordlessly, a form of love that required no reply. Savannah took grapes. She thought: the college wants its yield, and I want something I haven't even named yet, and those are not the same want, and one of them is mine.

"Okay," she said aloud. "Here's where I've landed. If the answer is yes, I'll go, because I made that deal and it's a good school and I'm not going to pretend I don't want it. But I'm allowed to want the other life too. Both things can be true. I just won't know which one I actually prefer until one of them happens, and that's fine, or at least it's the situation."

"That's not fine," Kelly said. "That's litotes."

"That is not what litotes is."

"'Not fine' for 'a slow-rolling catastrophe.' Understatement for emphasis. Look it up."

"I don't need to look it up, I know what it means, I'm just disappointed you used it on me." She was smiling, though. Under the smile, the two engines kept running.

At four fifty-eight she opened the portal. Kelly stood behind her chair with a grape raised like a tiny toast. The screen loaded the way screens load when they know something, taking their time, and Savannah read the first line of the decision, and put her hand over her mouth, and Kelly shouted loud enough to frighten the grapes off the table.

"So?" said Kelly. "Which is it?"

Savannah scrolled down to find the deposit deadline.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: The World Health Organization recommends adults eat less than 2 grams of sodium a day, which is less than 5 grams of salt, to help lower blood pressure.
story:
The cuff hissed and tightened around her grandmother's arm until the fingers went slightly gray, then released with a shudder, and Alice copied the numbers onto the back of an envelope before they vanished from the little screen. One forty-eight over ninety-four. She had volunteered for this, sort of; Mr. Nair had assigned each of them in health class a household member to track for two weeks, and since her mother worked nights and her grandfather was dead, the grandmother it was. The trouble was that the numbers meant nothing to her yet. They sat on the envelope like coordinates for a country she had never seen.

"Too high," her grandmother said, not asking, and turned back to the stove, where a pot of soup from a can was already steaming. "The doctor says the same. He gives me pills and tells me to walk."

Alice turned the can over. Sodium, per serving: nine hundred milligrams. She dug the envelope out again and did the arithmetic twice, because it seemed wrong. The can said it held about two and a half servings. If her grandmother ate half the pot, as she usually did, with the saltines she crumbled on top, that was over a gram of sodium in a single sitting. She remembered the figure Mr. Nair had made them write at the top of their notebooks, the one half the class had groaned at: the World Health Organization said adults should eat less than two grams of sodium a day, which was less than five grams of salt, to help lower blood pressure. She had assumed that limit would be hard to break. Now it looked like something you could do before lunch.

"You're counting something," her grandmother said. "You get your father's face when you count."

"The salt. In the soup. It's a lot of it." Alice said it carefully, because she had already learned, from past skirmishes over butter and cigarettes, that walking into this kitchen with health advice was like walking in with an inspection notice. Her grandmother's generation, her mother said, had survived wars and rationing and did not appreciate being stigmatized at their own table, lectured as if every meal were a verdict.

"Soup is soup," her grandmother said. "I have eaten it my whole life."

"Maybe not this much of it, though. Maybe not every day." Alice heard her own tone sharpen and pulled it back. "There's a lower-sodium one at the store. Same brand. I looked."

Her grandmother laughed, a short sound, not unkind. "And it tastes like the box it came in. Don't be facetious with me about my groceries."

"I'm not joking. I'm actually not." And she wasn't; that was the strange part. She had started this assignment to get the marks, and somewhere between the envelope and the can she had started to care, though she could not have said exactly when. "Look. Two grams a day. That's the whole limit, for everything, and this one bowl is half of it. That's not me being dramatic. That's just the label."

Her grandmother sat down, which she rarely did while the stove was on, and took the envelope from Alice's hand. She looked at the numbers there, the blood pressure first, then the sodium sums, her lips moving slightly over Alice's rounded arithmetic. Alice watched her and thought, with an honesty she kept to herself, that she did not actually know whether the soup was the cause of anything. Two grams was the rule, the reading was the fact, but the distance between the two, the body's private accounting, was something no envelope could show her. Maybe the walking mattered more. Maybe the pills. She held both possibilities open, the way Mr. Nair kept insisting they should, and did not pretend to close them.

"Tomorrow," her grandmother said at last, "you come with me to the store. You pick the soup. If it is terrible, we tell no one." She tapped the envelope once against the table, a small gavel, and Alice understood she was being granted clemency in both directions: the past meals forgiven, the future ones not yet on trial.

"And Saturday," Alice said, standing to stir the pot before it boiled over, "I'll walk with you. Around the block first, then maybe to the park. Mr. Nair says even regular walks bring the numbers down, and we'll take the reading again after and see." She turned the burner low, took the spoon, and began to stir.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: By the second derivative test, if f'(a) = 0 and f''(a) is negative, the function has a local maximum at x = a.
story:
The screen door of his grandfather's house still caught halfway and had to be lifted, a trick Nolan had learned before he could read. He set his backpack on the kitchen chair where the vinyl had split decades ago, took out his notebook, and spread it flat beside the jar of pencils that had stood on the same windowsill since his father was sixteen. Upstairs, his grandfather was napping, which meant the house belonged to Nolan and the afternoon.

The assignment was due Monday, and Ms. Wiśniewski had written one comment at the top of his first attempt, in green ink: "You found the critical point. Now: is it a peak or a valley?" Nolan had stared at that sentence on the bus until the letters stopped meaning anything. The function was something small and harmless, a polynomial modeling the profit of a student-run coffee cart, and at x = 3 the derivative went to zero, exactly as the problem intended. Somewhere near x = 3, the cart either made its best money or its worst, and Nolan could not tell which.

He had texted Sophia from the bus. She answered now, three hours later, while he sat at the kitchen table copying the function onto a clean page. "skipped math, went to the lake," she wrote, "but my cousin says differentiate again. like, do the derivative of the derivative." Then, a second message: "she says it's called the second derivative test." Nolan read it twice, set the phone face down, and pulled the pencil jar closer.

Differentiating twice felt almost rude, like asking a question of an answer. The first derivative had told him where the slope flattened to nothing; the second seemed tangential to the point, a fact about curvature when what he wanted was height. Still, Sophia's cousin had never steered her wrong on anything, so he worked it through. The original function was a polynomial, and polynomials differentiated obediently, each term stepping down a degree, the numbers shrinking as they went. He wrote the second derivative at the bottom of the page and substituted 3.

The result came out negative. He checked the arithmetic twice, because the number was small and a dropped sign would flip everything. It stayed negative, and he sat with that for a moment, pencil hovering. Somewhere in his notes from Tuesday was a fragment he'd half-heard while Byron leaned across the aisle asking to borrow a ruler: negative meant the curve was bending downward, concave like a frown. If the slope was zero and the curve was bending downward, then the point wasn't a floor. It was a ceiling. At x = 3, the coffee cart hit its local maximum, and every cart-load on either side earned less. He underlined it, then felt foolish for underlining it and underlined it anyway.

The stairs announced his grandfather before he appeared, the fourth step still complaining. He came down in his cardigan with his glasses pushed up on his forehead, went straight to the kettle, and only then noticed the papers. He stood behind Nolan's chair and read for a long time, one hand on the table's edge.

"Three years of this at the technical institute," he said finally. "Before the war, after it, we never called it calculus. We called it finding the tops of hills." He tapped the second derivative with one finger. "You did this yourself?"

"Sophia's cousin told me the name of it," Nolan said. "The second derivative test. But I did the part with the numbers."

His grandfather made a sound that could have been approval or the kettle. He filled the pot, and while the water heated he pulled a chair around and sat, not at the table exactly but beside it, angling himself toward the notebook the way he angled toward the evening news. "Your grandmother ascribed every good grade in this house to the kitchen table," he said. "Poor lighting, good table. She thought the two went together." It was a tangential thing to say, and Nolan recognized it as the kind of thing his grandfather said instead of saying he was pleased.

Down in the cellar, where Nolan went to look for more pencils, he found the shelves his grandfather had never let anyone tidy: fossils and beach stones sorted into cigar boxes with taped labels, brachiopods and trilobites lined up in rows. The labels were in his grandfather's hand, older and steadier than the hand on the grocery list upstairs, and one box read simply "PHYLUM BRACHIOPODA," spelled out in capital letters as if the word itself were an object you could keep. Nolan held the box under the bulb. Every creature in it had been sorting itself into categories for four hundred million years, and here was his grandfather still sorting, still deciding what belonged with what. He put the box back exactly where its dust shadow said it had been.

Upstairs he reworked the whole problem from the beginning, and this time the doubt didn't come. He wrote the first derivative, solved for zero, wrote the second derivative, evaluated it at 3, saw the negative sign, and stated the maximum with a calm he did not entirely trust, so he did it once more with the constant changed to see whether the reasoning survived. It did. The peak moved a little to the left, as it should, and the second derivative came out negative again, as it should, and the ceiling stayed a ceiling.

He photographed the page for Sophia, with the note "your cousin was right," and carried his grandfather a cup of tea. The old man took it without looking away from the window, where the light had gone long and low across the yard, and Nolan sat down across from him and turned his notebook around so the page faced outward, the negative number circled once, the word maximum written beside it in his own handwriting.

"There," his grandfather said, tapping the window instead of the page. "The sun does that in December. Same idea." Nolan looked out at the fence post throwing its shadow, longer now than it had been an hour ago, and knew this was not quite right, that the sun was not a polynomial, but he let it stand.

"Basically," he said, and drank his tea.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A food bank is usually a central warehouse that collects and distributes food to local agencies, while a food pantry is where people pick up food directly.
story:
Vanessa arrived at the chain-link gate of the community garden at eight-forty, ten minutes early, holding a paper bag of oranges her mother had pushed into her hands at the door. A folding table stood near the toolshed with a clipboard on it, and a man in a green polo shirt waved her over. Behind him, volunteers moved crates of canned tomatoes and rice from a van into the low cinderblock building at the back of the lot.

"You must be Vanessa," the man said. "I'm Mr. Lombardi. You're on inventory today. Mostly weighing and logging."

She had signed up because her college application was already in and she needed something to do with her Saturdays, though she had written "give back to the community" on the interest form, and she was aware those two reasons did not sit easily together. She said good morning and took the clipboard.

By ten the crates were stacked in rows along the walls, and Vanessa had learned to tare the scale and to write the weight before the number vanished from the display. Aden, a boy she recognized from her econ class, worked beside her, calling out weights. Between crates he asked why nobody had come in for food yet.

"Because it doesn't work like that here," said Hamzah, a volunteer in a red apron who had been coming since spring. "This is the food bank. It's the central warehouse that collects the food and distributes it to local agencies. The pantry is where people actually pick up groceries."

"Then where's the pantry?" Aden asked.

"Church basement on Fourth Street. There's another one by the school. Trucks from here supply them."

Aden looked at the stacked crates as though they had misled him. Vanessa wrote 14.2 in the column for canned beans and thought about her own assumption, which had been the same as his. She had pictured lines of people at this gate. In her head the whole thing had been simpler and, she noticed now, more flattering to her, as if handing someone an orange was the point rather than the last step of a longer chain.

The morning produced its one real crisis around eleven. A driver arrived with a donation from a grocery chain, forty boxes of yogurt with a sell-by date printed in a format nobody recognized. Mr. Lombardi bent over a box, then straightened and asked whether anyone could confirm the dates were still good. Hamzah said the pantry wouldn't take them without verification. Aden suggested calling the store. Vanessa, who had spent an hour that week arguing with a chatbot about a refund, said the veracity of the dates could probably be checked against the store's own online inventory system, and Mr. Lombardi handed her his phone.

She found the product page, matched the lot code, and confirmed the yogurt had two weeks left. Mr. Lombardi wrote it on the donation slip and told her she had just saved forty boxes from the compost. Hamzah carried the first box to the truck going to Fourth Street. Vanessa followed with two more, and when she set them down a woman from the pantry, thin, in a windbreaker, thanked her without ceremony and counted the boxes out loud.

The woman stayed to drink the coffee someone had put out, and she and Hamzah argued mildly about whether the garden plot beside the shed should grow food for the pantry or flowers for the neighborhood association. Hamzah said flowers were parochial, a nice word for a nice neighborhood, while the pantry served three zip codes. The woman said people needed something to look at too, and that children from Fourth Street came to see the sunflowers every July. Neither gave in. Vanessa drank her coffee and found she could hold both positions at once without choosing, or at least without choosing yet, though she was honest enough to admit that holding two ideas was easier than deciding between them, and that deciding was probably what someone would eventually have to do.

At noon the oranges were still in the paper bag by the gate. She had imagined handing them over, one by one, and now she understood they would go into a crate, onto a truck, to a church basement, into a bag a stranger would carry home. It was a worse picture for her and a better one for the oranges. She carried the bag inside anyway and set it on the intake table. Mr. Lombardi weighed it without comment and said, "Two point one. Write it down."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The Common Application, which lets US college applicants send one application to many schools, was founded in 1975 with 15 member colleges and now has more than 1,000 members.
story:
The library on Marlow Street kept its college brochures on a metal carousel near the copying machine, and Luke had turned that carousel so many times this spring that the pages had gone soft at the corners. He came in on a Tuesday afternoon in March, three days after the email had said his application was complete and under review, and he sat down at the computer nearest the window with his backpack still on one shoulder, as if he might leave at any moment.

He opened his account and looked at the green check marks. Everything submitted, everything received, everything waiting. There was nothing new to read, but he read it anyway, scrolling through the list of schools he had applied to as though one of them might have blinked.

"You're going to wear a hole in that chair," Erica said. She dropped her books on the table beside him and sat down without asking. She had a study guide open before her coat was fully off. "Walter's over in the biography section pretending to research his English paper. He's actually reading about shark attacks."

"I'm not obsessing," Luke said. "I'm checking."

"Those are the same thing right now."

He didn't argue. He had done the whole application at the kitchen table in January, his mother refilling his coffee twice without being asked, and he remembered the moment halfway through when he'd realized he only had to enter his grades and his essay and his activities once. His cousin had told him horror stories from years back, or maybe from a different country, about writing to each school separately, twenty envelopes, twenty versions of the same self. "It's called the Common Application," his cousin had said, and Luke had looked it up: fifteen member colleges when it started in 1975, and now more than a thousand of them, all taking that one form. He had felt something almost like gratitude toward whoever had thought of it, some committee of tired people in the seventies deciding that eighteen-year-olds deserved a small mercy.

"I keep thinking there's something I should be doing," he said now. "Some letter, some call, some way of making them want me more. And there isn't. It's just time."

Erica tapped her pencil against her study guide. "Then do time. Do your homework during time. That's what I'm doing, and I'm on the same carousel you are." She was waiting too, for a different school, and she said it without drama, which somehow made it heavier. Walter wandered over with his shark book and put it down as a cushion for his chin.

"Walter," Luke said, "did you apply anywhere you actually want to go, or anywhere that would take you?"

Walter considered this with the seriousness of a boy who had spent twenty minutes on sharks. "Both, I think. Those aren't opposite things." He paused. "Maybe that's a lie. I don't know yet which one I said yes to first."

Luke turned back to the screen. He had told everyone, including himself, that he wanted the big school with the engineering program, the one whose rejection would sting the most and whose acceptance would look the best announced at dinner. But there was a smaller one, third on his list, that he had written about in his supplemental essay with an ease that had surprised him, sentences that came out finished. He had been treating the whole thing like a machine with one correct output. Maybe it was more like Walter's answer: two motives running at once, neither one fully honest, neither one exactly a subterfuge. He tried to recalibrate, to imagine himself at the small school in September, and found he could picture the dining hall, the walk to class, the specific weight of being nobody there yet. The picture did not frighten him. That was information, even if it wasn't an answer.

The librarian came by with a cart of returns, and Luke closed his account and helped her slide the college brochures back into their slots on the carousel, the one for the big school and the one for the small one ending up side by side, spines touching. His phone buzzed once in his pocket, and he stood there with his hand on it, not taking it out, while Erica watched him from the table.

"It's probably your mom," she said.

"I know." He took it out anyway. It was a text from his mother, asking if he'd be home for dinner. He typed yes, put the phone away, and went back to sit with them, sliding his chair in until its legs scraped softly on the old tile floor.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA recommends eating refrigerated cooked leftovers within three to four days, which limits how far ahead a week of meals can be cooked without freezing some.
story:
The kitchen still smelled of her grandfather's coffee, though he had been dead since March, and Alexandra stood in front of the open refrigerator wondering whether that was grief or just a house that held onto things. Her grandmother had offered the kitchen to her for the summer, one condition attached: Alexandra would plan the meals, shop for them, cook them. "Your mother did the same at your age," her grandmother said, peeling an orange at the table with slow, deliberate hands. "I am too old to feed you and too stubborn to let you buy those noodle cups."

So on Sunday morning Alexandra spread a notebook across the counter and began. Seven days, five lunches each for herself and Rachael, who had offered twenty dollars a week and a shared enthusiasm for anything that involved containers. Alexandra liked the arithmetic of it. Rice on Monday and Tuesday, pasta Wednesday, a bean stew Thursday, and then she stopped writing, because the pasta sauce and the stew would both be sitting in the refrigerator by then, and something about that bothered her in a way she could not yet name.

"Grandma," she called, "how long can you keep cooked food in the fridge before it goes off?"

Her grandmother considered the ceiling. "Ask your phone. I kept things longer than I should have for forty years and I am still here, which proves nothing."

The search took a minute. The USDA, an official page with a chart, recommended eating refrigerated cooked leftovers within three to four days. Alexandra read it twice, and the problem she had half-sensed assembled itself fully: if she cooked everything on Sunday, the last lunches of the week would be five, six, seven days old. Too old. The week could not simply be cooked in one long Sunday afternoon; some of it would have to wait, or go somewhere colder. She opened the freezer compartment and found it crammed with her grandfather's bagged tomatoes from a summer before last, each one labelled in his cramped handwriting, and she stood there for a while, not moving the tomatoes yet.

She had come here in April, straight after the funeral, and found him in the garden already, in a sense, because the tomato stakes were in and the string was tied and there was nothing to do about it. Her grandmother had handed her a trowel without a word. That was the first time she understood that a person could keep working a plan made by someone who was gone, and that it was not morbid, it was maintenance. Now she lifted the tomatoes out one bag at a time and stacked them on the counter, making room, and her grandmother looked over and said, "Good. We'll make sauce on Wednesday," as if Alexandra had done all this on purpose.

At the market on Monday, Alexandra walked the aisles with a list she had rewritten twice in the car. She had been raised, loosely, on the assumption that money was a weather system, sometimes rainy, sometimes not discussed. Her grandmother shopped like a woman who had known penurious years and had never stopped respecting them, weighing the beans in her palm before committing, and Alexandra caught herself doing the same. "You're counting," her grandmother observed.

"I'm calculating solvency," Alexandra said. "Rachael's twenty dollars, minus the pork shoulder, minus, like, existence."

"Rachael. The loud one or the one who cried at the poetry thing?"

"There's one Rachael, Grandma."

They bought what was on the list and, at the register, one unplanned bag of clementines, because some principles exist to be betrayed gently.

Mr. Choi from next door was watering his sidewalk plants when they carried the bags in, and he asked what all the containers were for. Alexandra, pleased to have a plan worth describing, started to expatiate on batch cooking, the Sunday prep, the five lunches, and then stopped herself mid-sentence, one hand still holding the pork. "Except I can't cook it all at once," she said. "The USDA says eat refrigerated leftovers within three to four days. So Sunday's food only carries me to Wednesday or Thursday."

Mr. Choi nodded slowly. "My mother froze everything. Soup for the apocalypse."

"So Thursday and Friday's lunches have to be cooked midweek, or frozen." Saying it aloud, she heard the small seam in her own logic: freezing the Sunday stew would save it, but she had never once thawed anything successfully, and her grandmother's microwave had a dial instead of buttons, like an instrument from another century. Was a plan you couldn't execute still a plan? She decided it was a draft.

She cooked Sunday: rice, roasted vegetables, the first batch of sauce, her grandmother drifting in and out, correcting nothing, which was its own form of teaching. On Wednesday they made the second sauce from the freezer tomatoes, and it tasted faintly of a summer Alexandra half-remembered, and she ladled it into containers and wrote the date on each lid in her grandfather's cramped hand without quite meaning to imitate it.

Thursday evening Rachael texted: lunch tomorrow? and Alexandra replied with a photograph of the containers, dated, ordered, the Thursday ones from the front of the fridge and the Friday ones, frozen since Sunday, now thawing in a bowl of water on the counter, exactly as the internet had instructed, though she would not know until noon whether she had done it right.

She turned the container over once, feeling the ice shift inside it, and set it back down to wait.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: Near the end of the development, a retransition often dwells on the home key's dominant chord, building an expectation that the tonic and the first theme are about to return.
story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and old paper, and Ms. Gallagher had cleared a workbench for Leah's books. A turntable sat at one end beside a crate of records, and Leah had claimed it every Tuesday since September, because at home her mother watched television in the only quiet room. Ms. Gallagher, who was seventy and had taught piano for forty years, left the garage door open an inch and said Leah could play anything as long as she lifted the needle carefully.

Leah's problem was specific. On Friday she had to mark, in the score of Mozart's Sonata in A major, K. 331, the first movement's exposition, development, and recapitulation, and hand the marked score to Mr. Rowan, who graded analysis at the conservatory prep program. She had failed the first attempt on a Haydn movement in October. She had circled a recapitulation where there was only a half cadence, and Mr. Rowan had written "expectation is not arrival" in the margin in green pen, and she had kept the page in her binder like evidence.

Iris came on the third Tuesday of November, carrying two cans of soda and her own agenda. "I need fifteen minutes of your time for the winter showcase," she said. "Amari's outside arguing with himself about whether to come in." Iris wanted Leah to play piano at the showcase, four hands with her, and Leah had been dodging the question for two weeks. Iris called this dodging, in her words, "a lifestyle."

Amari did come in, holding the door frame. "Your garage is colder than the hallway," he said. "Which is an achievement." He sat on an overturned milk crate and watched Leah open the score on the workbench. Amari couldn't read music, and he said so without apology; he refused to let it stigmatize him, he said, the way it had in sixth grade when a choir teacher had moved him to the back row for humming. Iris, who called most classical music "museum furniture," had once called Mozart "elevator music with a wig," and Leah had told her that was a dysphemism, and Iris had said, "Fine, it's beautiful elevator music," which was her way of conceding.

Leah put the record on. "I'm going to play the whole movement," she said. "You two just listen. Tell me what you hear, especially near the end of the middle part." She had her pencil ready over the score. The exposition was easy; the theme was stated, then stated again in the dominant key, and she bracketed both with steady strokes. The development she had marked too early last time, and this time she watched the measure numbers and listened for the moment the theme stopped being itself.

Amari leaned forward about a minute into that middle section. The harmony had gone restless, the left hand circling, and then it settled onto one repeating harmony, urgent and leaning, and Amari said, "There, it's coming back, right? The opening tune. It's about to start over." He actually lifted his hand as if to hold the sound in place.

Leah found the measure. The harmony was the dominant of the home key, and it held there, repeating, building, and she did not write "recapitulation" beside it. "Not yet," she said. "That's what I got wrong on Haydn." She remembered the green ink. Near the end of the development, the music could dwell on the home key's dominant chord, and it built the expectation that the tonic and the first theme were about to return, and that dwelling was real and long, and the return itself was still measures away. Amari had heard the promise, not the fulfillment. She wrote a bracket and the word "retransition" beside it, and underlined it twice.

"That's called the retransition," she said to Amari, pointing at the bracket. "You just heard one."

"I heard the tune coming back," Amari said.

"It hadn't come back yet. That's the trick of it." She let the record run, and the dominant held, and Amari stayed leaning forward, and then the theme arrived, whole and quiet, exactly where the first measure had begun, and Leah drew the heaviest bracket of the evening. She sat back. She was not certain, even now, that her exposition boundary at the repeat sign was what Mr. Rowan wanted, and she was honest with herself about that; the retransition she would defend to anyone.

Iris waited until the movement ended, then set her soda can down on the workbench with a small deliberate click. "Showcase," she said. "I'm not letting it go. I've asked you three times and you keep hiding in here with a dead Austrian." Ms. Gallagher, who had appeared in the doorway somewhere in the last minute, said nothing about any of it; she crossed to the turntable and adjusted the tonearm with two fingers, frowning at the dust.

Leah looked at her bracketed score, then at Iris. "Tuesday and Thursday I'm in here," she said. "Saturday I could practice the duet." Iris's face opened like a window. Amari stood up from the milk crate and pointed at the score. "Play the part where it fakes you out again," he said. "I want to hear if it fools me twice."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Social loafing, the drop in effort people make in groups, shrinks when each member's individual contribution can be identified.
story:
Nathan had always considered himself the hardest worker on the Riverview Raptors, a claim he made often and with real conviction, usually while lacing his skates. The rink at six a.m. smelled like cold rubber and old coffee, and Nathan liked to arrive first, or at least to remember arriving first, and to note who was still in the parking lot when the zamboni finished. William was always late. Kiara was always early but, in Nathan's private accounting, somehow not really early. Nathan kept these assessments in his head the way other people kept grudges, warm and well fed.

The problem was the team. They were four games into the season and had lost three, and it wasn't Nathan's fault. He was clear on this. The forwards coasted on the backcheck. The defensemen glided through gap drills like men on a leisure tour of a frozen lake. At the third practice after a 6-1 loss, Coach stood at the bench with a clipboard and said nothing at all, which was worse than yelling.

After practice, Nathan and William sat in the bleachers eating fries from the rink snack bar, which Ms. Smith, who ran the concession, sold them at a discount because they were, in her words, the only two who ever said thank you. William, who read things, who had opinions about everything Nathan did, said, "You know what this is? Social loafing. The drop in effort people make in groups."

"That's not a thing," Nathan said.

"It's a thing. It shrinks when each person's contribution can be identified." William bit a fry. "Like, if everyone knows your numbers."

Nathan said nothing, because he had spent the first fifteen minutes of backcheck drills at roughly the speed of a man being pulled by a very slow dog, and the idea that this might be visible, attributable, named, was unwelcome. He had been predicating his whole self-image on the assumption that effort was invisible, a private virtue registered somewhere by the universe. It was, he now suspected, not axiomatic.

What Nathan did not see, and what the reader should know, is that from the ice, people could see him. Kiara, who played wing and had watched Nathan lecture the second line about backchecking while himself gliding, noticed everything. She noticed the way he slowed when Coach looked away and sped up when Coach looked at him, a small act of arbitrage, trading effort for attention whenever the exchange rate favored it.

She brought it up in the locker room, not cruelly, but not gently either. "You talk like you're the only one who tries," she said, pulling her helmet on. "We can all see you coast."

"I don't coast," said Nathan, who was, at that moment, coasting in a more general sense, through the season, through the argument, through his own story about himself.

Coach's solution, when it came, was a whiteboard. He hung it behind the bench with every player's name and every sprint time from every drill, updated daily, visible to anyone who walked past the rink, including Ms. Smith, who read it over her coffee and gave the slowest skaters extra-large portions out of what Nathan assumed was pity. The first day of the whiteboard, William ran the endurance drill in a time that would have gotten him cut a week earlier. Kiara shaved two seconds. The second-line center, a boy Nathan had privately written off, beat them all, and stood there breathing hard with the surprised face of someone meeting himself for the first time. Nathan looked at his own name, at his own mediocre column of numbers, and understood that the whiteboard had done in one afternoon what his speeches had never done, and that the speeches had mostly been for the parts of him nobody could see.

At the next game they won, 3-2, and Nathan had an assist, which he described afterward in the parking lot as "basically a goal." Kiara let him have it. William ate another order of fries and said, "Whiteboard's gone next week, Coach said. Budget." Nobody said anything for a moment. They stood in the cold outside the rink, breath hanging in the air, and Nathan looked back through the glass at the empty ice where the zamboni was making its slow, patient pass.

"Times are still going up on the team chat," Kiara said. "Every player, every drill."

"Individually," William said.

"Yeah," Nathan said. "Individually." He picked up his bag and shouldered the door open, and the three of them walked in out of the cold.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: The 17th edition of the Chicago Manual of Style, published in 2017, began discouraging 'ibid.' in favor of shortened citations that repeat the author and a short title.
story:
Hunter's grandfather had shipped him the style guide in a padded envelope with a note that read, in his engineer's block capitals, THIS WILL SEE YOU THROUGH. The book was older than Hunter's mother. It smelled like a basement that had survived a flood, and on page 112, underlined twice in blue ballpoint, was the word that had cost Hunter eleven points: ibid.

He spread the evidence out on the library table like a crime scene. The returned paper, bleeding red ink. The grandfather's guide. And, at his elbow, the library's own copy of the Chicago Manual of Style, 17th edition, so new the spine still cracked when he opened it. Alyssa slid into the chair across from him and set down her coffee, which had begun to coagulate into something that resembled road tar.

"Mr. MacLeod wrote a paragraph on yours," she said. "Mine just has a frowny face."

"Where's yours?" She turned her laptop so he could see the screen. Her footnotes were clean, identical in shape, each one repeating the author's last name and a short title like patient little soldiers. He compared them to his own, which dwindled after the first citation into a trail of ibids, ibids, and one ibid., 214, which he had felt quite clever about at two in the morning.

Rosaly arrived late, as always, carrying a bag of clementines she distributed like a diplomat. She leaned over Hunter's paper and tapped the margin where Mr. MacLeod had written see CMoS 17. "What's that mean?"

"Seventeenth edition," Hunter said. "This one." He pulled the library's copy toward him and started hunting through the index, which was its own small education. He found the entry, then the section, then the sentence. The 17th edition, published in 2017, had begun discouraging ibid. in favor of shortened citations that repeated the author and a short title. He read it twice. The word he'd underlined, the word his grandfather had underlined, had been retired, quietly, without a funeral.

"So my grandfather's book is wrong?"

"It's not wrong," Rosaly said, peeling a clementine in one long spiral, a talent Hunter had never mastered. "It's old."

This distinction occupied him for a while. His grandfather was not a dilettante about these things. The man kept logs of furnace filters and filed his tax receipts by month. If the guide said ibid., then ibid. had been right, in its season, the way rotary phones had been right. And Mr. MacLeod was not wrong either. Hunter looked at Alyssa's footnotes again, all those repeated names and short titles, redundant by his grandfather's standards, wasteful even, and yet perfectly clear. A reader could land on any one of them at random and know exactly where it came from. The ibid. only worked if you'd been paying attention from the start. It assumed an orderly reader moving through an orderly paper, and it punished everyone else.

He opened his laptop and started the revision. It was not difficult work, only humble work, the kind where you retype your own sentences with slightly different furniture. Where the paper had said ibid., he typed Rossi, Brief History, and where it had said ibid., 214, he typed Rossi, Brief History, 214. Alyssa worked beside him on her own paper, and Rosaly, who had finished hers a week early and refused to feel bad about it, read a novel with a cover so saturnine that it looked like it was in mourning.

Mr. MacLeod appeared at four o'clock, doing his slow circuit of the reference section, stopping at tables the way a doctor makes rounds. When he reached theirs, Hunter pushed the paper toward him.

"I found the seventeenth edition," Hunter said. "It discourages ibid. Now, instead, you repeat the author and a short title."

Mr. MacLeod looked at the revision, then at the old guide still sitting open on the table, its underlining exposed. He picked it up, weighed it in one hand, and set it back down without comment.

"My grandfather's," Hunter said.

"He taught you to cite, though," Mr. MacLeod said. "Half the battle." He moved on toward the periodicals, where a boy was sleeping on a copy of National Geographic.

Hunter looked at the old guide for a moment longer. He would not tell his grandfather about the eleventh edition's fate, or the red ink, or the eleven points. He would tell him the paper got an A minus, and that the footnotes were impeccable, and both statements would be true. He closed the grandfather's book gently, the way you close a door on someone sleeping, and slid it into his backpack next to the new one.

Rosaly held out the last clementine across the table. "You're keeping both?"

"I'm keeping both."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: Google added 'search by image' in 2011, letting users upload a picture or paste its link to find where else it appears on the web.
story:
The video arrived in the family group chat at six in the morning, forwarded by Nevaeh's grandmother with the message "PRAY FOR THEM." It showed a flooded street, a man on a roof holding a dog, brown water dragging a car sideways past a mailbox. By the time Nevaeh got to third period, the same clip had surfaced on three separate accounts under three separate dates, each claiming it was happening right now, somewhere different.

The computer lab smelled like floor wax and thirty bodies' worth of Tuesday. Ms. Mokoena had posted the assignment on the board, media literacy, verify before you share, and most people were clicking through it the way you click through anything, torpid, half asleep, screensaver faces. Nevaeh sat down next to Kadence, who had the video open on her phone and was composing a repost caption.

"Wait," Nevaeh said. "Before you send that."

"It's a guy on a roof. With a dog. What's to verify, his suffering?"

"I don't know yet. That's the point." Ms. Mokoena had put a link on the assignment page, something about Google's search by image, which she said had existed since 2011, letting users upload a picture or paste its link to find where else it appears on the web. Nevaeh had never used it. She paused the video at the clearest frame, the man, the dog, the mailbox, saved the image, and dragged it into the search box the way you'd drag a file into a folder, half expecting nothing.

The results loaded while Rafael leaned over from the next station, chewing a pen cap. The earliest hit was a news article from six years ago. Then a weather service page. Then a fundraising appeal, also old, with the same man, same dog, same mailbox, in a story about a different flood entirely. One of the "happening now" accounts had cropped the timestamp out of the corner.

"So it's real, it's just old," Kadence said, which Nevaeh thought was a genuinely interesting distinction and also not what her grandmother had been told. She opened the group chat, started typing a reply, and stopped. Her grandmother had forwarded it to fourteen people, some of whom were deacons. There was a version of the message Nevaeh could send, the you got played version, which Kadence was already drafting on her own phone for her own followers, funny and merciless. There was another version, which she couldn't quite get to, that would tell her grandmother the truth without making her feel like the last person on earth allowed to be fooled.

"Grandma's not going to do a reverse image search," Rafael said, reading her screen without asking, which was its own problem, but she let it go. "She types with one finger."

"She forwarded a thing about a kidney theft ring in 2019," Nevaeh said. "I sent her a fact check and she replied with a smiley face and then forwarded the same thing again two months later."

"That's the denouement of every fact check," Kadence said. "Nothing changes, credits roll."

Ms. Mokoena moved through the rows, hands behind her back, and paused at their station long enough to see the search results still open. "Nice work," she said, and Nevaeh noticed she didn't say what the work was worth, whether the man on the roof had been helped or harmed by six more years of circulation, whether an old true image in new false clothing was better or worse than a new false image altogether. The assignment wanted a paragraph on the ethics of sharing. Nevaeh had two ideas that wouldn't sit in the same paragraph: that slowing down mattered, and that slowing down had just cost her a nice feeling she couldn't get back, the feeling of praying for someone, even someone six years gone from that roof.

She typed to her grandmother: "The video is real but it's from 2019, not now. I can show you how I checked." Then she deleted "from 2019," retyped it, deleted it again. Rafael went back to his pen cap. Kadence hit send on her merciless caption and exhaled like she'd finished a race. Nevaeh left the draft unsent, copied the link to the search, and pasted it underneath the sentence so it sat there, waiting.

"Try 'the dog is fine now,'" Rafael offered.

"Is the dog fine now?"

"No idea," he said, and turned back to his own screen.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Gar Alperovitz argued in Atomic Diplomacy (1965) that the atomic bombs were used on Japan partly to intimidate the Soviet Union.
story:
The assignment on the board read: "Two historians, one question. Who is right about the bombs?" Seth had copied it into his notebook before the bell finished ringing, and by lunch he was still staring at it, because the two historians in question appeared to disagree about everything except the date.

"So what's the actual fight?" Jean-Felix asked, dropping his tray beside Seth's in the cafeteria. He had a way of asking questions that sounded like dares.

Seth opened his binder. "Ms. Zhao gave us this guy Gar Alperovitz. He wrote a book in 1965 called Atomic Diplomacy, and he argued the atomic bombs were used on Japan partly to intimidate the Soviet Union. That's the claim. There's another historian in the packet, more traditional, who says the bombs ended the war, full stop."

"So one says they were the last act of World War Two and the other says the first act of the Cold War," Jean-Felix said, spearing a fry. "That's actually a cool way to put it."

"That's the problem, though. It's too cool. It sounds like a poster." Seth turned to the photocopied pages. He had underlined so much in the first reading that the underlining meant nothing anymore. "Ms. Zhao wants us to weigh both against the evidence, and I keep just agreeing with whichever one I read last."

Micah slid into the seat across from them, earbuds still in, pulling one out when he saw the binder. "Is that the bombs essay? My cousin did it two years ago. He said half the class wrote that America was evil and the other half wrote that America could do no wrong, and Ms. Zhao failed everybody."

"Failed everybody?"

"Gave them all C's. Same thing." Micah put his earbud back in, then took it out again. "There's a thing at the war memorial downtown on Saturday. Vets talking about the Pacific. You could go be weird at old men."

Seth went. The memorial was a granite wall with names on it, and in front of it a small crowd of folding chairs, an empty podium, and a man in a navy cap talking to no one in particular about ships. Seth had brought his notebook and a sense of being out of place, and he stood at the edge until an older woman asked him if he was there for his grandfather.

"For a paper," he said, and felt the smallness of that.

He stayed anyway. After the speeches, he ended up next to the man in the navy cap, who asked him, in the way old men ask, what a sixteen-year-old wanted with all this. Seth explained the assignment, the two historians, the question of whether you could ever settle it.

"You want it settled," the man said. "That's a young man's want." He adjusted his cap. "My brother was on a ship in the Pacific, headed for the invasion. He used to say the bombs saved his life. Then he got older and started wondering about the Russians, about what Truman's people were thinking when they test-fired that thing before they'd even used it. He held both of those at once. Drove him a little crazy, but he held them."

Walking home past the shuttered hardware store, whose display window had been metamorphic to Seth since childhood, always showing some new version of the town, he thought about the man's brother. Not about who was right. About how a person could carry two answers in the same body.

On Monday he asked Ms. Zhao for the document packet again and read it differently, with a column ruled down the page. In the left column he put everything that supported Alperovitz, the claim from Atomic Diplomacy that the bombs were used partly to intimidate the Soviet Union. In the right, everything that fit the bombs-as-ending-the-war account. Some evidence went in both columns. Some went in neither. When Jean-Felix looked over his shoulder and said, "Dude, that's just a chart," Seth said, "It's the opposite. It's me deciding not to pretend it all points one way."

"But you have to pick a side," Jean-Felix said. "That's the assignment."

Seth wrote his essay that night, and this is what he wrote near the end: that the traditional view could absolve the decision only by ignoring the timing and the diplomacy around it, but that Alperovitz's reading, taken as the whole truth, absolved the other side of everything, and the evidence refused both favors. He argued that the bombings were probably both things at once, the last act of one war and the first move of the next, and that history did not come with clean edges just because he wanted them.

He got it back on Thursday with a grade he didn't show anyone, but at the bottom, under the score, Ms. Zhao had written one line in green ink: "This is the beginning of the argument, not the end of it. Come argue with me about paragraph six." He stood at her door, still holding the paper, and knocked.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a Passover Seder the youngest child present customarily asks the Four Questions from the Haggadah, beginning with 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
story:
The texts arrived while Logan was still in the driveway, phone tilted under his jacket so his mother wouldn't see. "Doors at 9. You said you'd come." Then, a minute later: "You're going to bail, aren't you." Coraly's band had their first real show tonight, a basement venue forty minutes from his grandmother's condo, and the Seder, his mother had reminded him twice in the car, started at six and did not run short.

Inside, the table was already set, the good plates polished to a shine. His uncle Saul arranged the matzah into its velvet pouch with the solemnity of a man defusing something. Arianna, eight and wearing tights with holes she insisted were intentional, stood at the far end of the table clutching a photocopied page from the Haggadah. She had been given a job, the same job Logan himself had been given nine years ago, and she looked like a defendant awaiting a verdict.

"I can't do it," she said, cornering him by the coat closet before the first cup of wine was even poured. "It's in front of everybody. In Hebrew parts. And English parts. There are four of them."

"There are four," Logan agreed. "But you only have to remember one thing to start." He took the page from her, held it low between them. "Why is this night different from all other nights? That's the opening. The whole thing opens with that question, and it's yours, because the youngest kid at the table is the one who asks. That's the custom. You're the youngest, so it's you."

Arianna's eyes went to the doorway, where their grandfather was hanging his coat, dour as February, which was his resting state. "What if I mess up the tune?"

"Then you've messed up the tune at a dinner where Uncle Saul once argued about tax law for an hour during the matzah break. The bar is on the floor." She laughed, which had been the plan, and he made her sing the first line into his shoulder, quiet, three times, until the words stopped shaking.

His phone buzzed against his hip. Coraly: "If you're not here by our third song I'm giving your ticket to Marcus. Marcus, Logan." He typed "trying," deleted it, typed "grandma's seder, family thing, told you," deleted that too, and finally sent nothing. He slid the phone into his coat pocket in the closet, next to Arianna's spare hair ribbons, and felt the loss of it like a pulled tooth.

The Seder ground forward through the plagues, Saul dipping his finger without enthusiasm, the salt water, the gefilte fish that Logan privately considered a trial of its own. His grandmother nudged the orange on the seder plate toward Arianna and told the old joke about the rabbi who said a woman belonged on the bimah like an orange on the seder plate, and how the community had answered by putting an orange there on purpose. The brisket was a reprieve from everyone's opinions about the brisket. When the door was opened for Elijah, cold April air moved through the room, and Logan watched the hallway, empty, and did not decide what he expected to see there.

Then it was time. Arianna stood. Her chair scraped. The room went quiet in that way that made quiet itself a kind of pressure, and she opened her mouth and said nothing. Five seconds. Ten. Logan raised his eyebrows at her, tapped his own chest twice, mouthing the words. Why is this night different from all other nights. Her chin came up. She sang it, small and true, all the way through the first question, and when she wobbled on the second he heard his grandfather's voice come in underneath hers, low and certain, carrying the melody the way you'd carry a kid across a flooded street. Their grandfather, who had not sung a note since the funeral. By the fourth question the two of them were in unison and the table had gone soft around the eyes.
