Later, during the hiding of the afikoman, Arianna tugged Logan into the hallway. "I didn't forget," she said.

"Forget what?"

"The words. I knew them from Purim prep. I did it on purpose." She looked back toward the dining room, where their grandfather was pretending not to watch the door. "Zayde only sings when somebody needs rescuing. So I needed rescuing."

Logan thought about his own doubt, the one he carried to this table every year and never named, and how it seemed suddenly possible to subsume it, not resolve it, just hold it inside something larger and older than his uncertainty. His phone was still in the closet. Coraly's show would be over in an hour.

"Hey," Arianna said. "Check the oven. Nobody ever checks the oven."

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: The Collingridge dilemma, from David Collingridge's 1980 book, says a technology's effects are hard to predict when it is new, but by the time they are clear it is hard to change.
story:
The group chat was called "lunch table (extended universe)," and by eleven on Tuesday night it had 214 messages. Someone had posted a screenshot from the school's new attendance app, the one that used the cameras outside the gym to log who came in late, and someone else had posted a screenshot of the school's code of conduct, and then everyone had started typing at once. Jack lay on his bed with his phone above his face, reading, not replying. He had a bio test tomorrow and a want that was smaller and sharper than the argument: he wanted to know whether he could still use the app to check his own attendance record without feeling like a hypocrite, because Ms. Hosseini had mentioned that a perfect attendance sheet would help his college recommendation, and his record had a mark on it from October that he knew was wrong.

The mark said he had cut fourth period on a day he had actually been in the nurse's office. He had gone to the office to fix it, and the secretary had said the system didn't take corrections from students, only from teachers, and his teacher had said the system didn't take corrections from teachers either, only from the district. Nobody at the district answered email. The mark sat there like a peccadillo he had committed, and the app made it visible to him daily, a small orange flag with his name attached.

Elena was typing in the chat. "the app flagged my brother 9 times last month. he works nights with my dad. it doesn't know what a job is."

Teo replied fast, as he always did. "or we could all just show up on time and the app would have nothing to say. people act like the software is the villain."

"it's not the villain," Elena typed. "it's a mirror somebody else aimed."

Jack watched the three dots appear and vanish under Elena's name, appear and vanish. He knew she was deleting the prolix version of her argument, the one with the statistics she had actually looked up, because Teo had once told her she argued like a court filing. She sent a shorter message instead: "come to the coffee shop tomorrow? i want to talk about this out loud, my thumbs are tired."

At the coffee shop on Wednesday, Elena had her laptop open to a page she had found at one in the morning. "Okay, so there's this guy," she said. "David Collingridge, 1980. He wrote a book. It's called the Collingridge dilemma. It says a technology's effects are hard to predict when it is new, but by the time they are clear it is hard to change."

Teo stirred his drink. "So we're in the second half already."

"Both halves," Elena said. "The app is new enough that nobody knows what it does, and old enough that everybody's already in it. That's the trap."

Jack turned his mug in its ring of condensation. He had been the quiet one at the table since they were twelve, the one who listened long enough to hear where two people were actually agreeing without noticing. "Teo, you said the software isn't the villain," he said. "Elena, you said it's a mirror somebody aimed. Those aren't opposites. If it's a mirror, then who aimed it matters, and how it was built matters, and whether we can still turn it matters."

Teo pointed his spoon at him. "You're doing the thing."

"I'm doing the thing," Jack admitted. "But listen. My attendance record has a wrong mark on it and no human can fix it. That's not a mirror. That's not even really software being bad. That's us deciding, somewhere, that automation was cheaper than listening, and then discovering we can't undo it without a district meeting nobody will schedule."

"So what do we do," Elena said, "if it's too early to know and too late to change?"

Jack said he didn't know. He said he had a test tomorrow and a recommendation riding on a record with a lie in it, and that the most honest thing he could do was use the system and complain about it at the same time, and that this bothered him more than either of their positions did.

On Thursday after the bio test, he walked past the gym cameras with his hood down, deliberately, a small private refusal to hide from something he hadn't agreed to. Then he went to Ms. Hosseini's room, where she was stacking papers, and asked whether she could mention in her letter that the October mark was wrong. She looked at him over her glasses and pulled a green pen toward her.

"I'll write that the system flagged you and the nurse's log says otherwise," she said. "Both facts, side by side. Let the admissions reader decide which one to valorize."

"That's fair," Jack said. "Though part of me wants to just fix the record."

She capped the pen. "Fix the record too, if you can. But the letter I can promise."

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) held that a public official suing for libel must prove actual malice: that the statement was known to be false or made with reckless disregard for truth.
story:
The community centre smelled of chlorine from the pool down the hall and burnt coffee from the vending machine, and Charlie had chosen a folding chair near the window because the light there made her notes look more official. Mr. Goldberg, who taught civics at the high school and judged the mock court every spring, sat behind a borrowed table with a gavel he never used. On the desk beside her, the case file: a fabricated newspaper had called a fabricated mayor corrupt, and the amount was wrong, and the question was whether the paper could be made to pay.

She had drawn the newspaper's side by lottery, which was the whole problem. She believed, privately and stubbornly, that a paper ought to check its facts. Taylor, arguing for the mayor, believed the same thing, which was why their preparation sessions in the centre's back room had curdled into something peevish and circular, two people agreeing with each other while pretending not to.

"You have to attack me," Taylor said, flipping a highlighter across the table. "You're being nice and it's ruining my practice."

"I'm building my case."

"You're stalling."

She was stalling. She had spent two evenings in the library with the real cases, the actual Supreme Court decisions in their grey government bindings, because Mr. Goldberg had told them the mock case was modelled on real doctrine and that anyone who argued from feeling alone would lose. She had found it on the third evening, in a case called New York Times v. Sullivan, 1964, and had read the holding three times before copying it onto an index card in her smallest handwriting. A public official suing for libel had to prove actual malice. "It's called actual malice," she said to Taylor now, sliding the card across the table. "The statement was known to be false, or made with reckless disregard for truth."

Taylor read the card twice. "But the paper got the number wrong. That's just false."

"That's not enough. That's what I'm saying. Read it again."

Taylor read it again, and Charlie watched the understanding arrive sideways, the way it does, a small shift in the shoulders rather than any lightbulb. "So my mayor has to prove they knew."

"Or didn't care whether it was true. Reckless disregard."

The subtext in the room changed after that. Taylor began arguing harder, louder, constructing hypotheticals in which the reporter had been told the number was wrong and printed it anyway, and Charlie understood that Taylor was no longer practising against her but against the doctrine itself, against the idea that a public figure should have to carry a heavier burden than anyone else. They stayed until the custodian flicked the hallway lights, and outside, in the parking lot, Taylor said, quietly, "My dad says the local paper misquotes him constantly. He's on the council. Nobody ever corrects it."

Charlie had not known that. She filed it somewhere and did not say the thing she might have said, which was that the doctrine was not about whether errors were fair but about whether a polity could afford to punish them, whether fear of lawsuits would desensitize editors to nothing at all except their own safety, until the paper printed only what no one could dispute, which was very little. She did not say it because she was not sure it was true in the clean way she wanted it to be true.

On the day of the mock argument, the pool had closed early and the hallway was silent. Mr. Goldberg sat with his hands folded. Charlie stood, laid out the sequence, the wrong figure, the correction printed two days later, and then the card's contents spoken without the card, actual malice defined the way the Court had defined it, known falsity or reckless disregard for truth. Taylor cross-examined with the father's unspoken grievance folded inside every question, and Charlie heard it, the second argument running underneath the first, and answered the surface one only, because that was the job.

Mr. Goldberg asked one question at the end, which he did every year. "Do you believe what you just argued?"

The room waited. Charlie looked at the index card, now soft at the corners, then at Taylor, who was not looking at her but at the mayor's name on the folder, the invented name of an invented official with a real complaint somewhere behind it. The window light had moved off her notes entirely and lay instead across the empty chairs where an audience would have been.

"Most of it," Charlie said. "The part I don't believe, I can't say which part it is yet."

Mr. Goldberg wrote something down, and the gavel sat untouched beside his hand.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Early Decision in US college admissions is binding: a student admitted with acceptable financial aid must enroll and withdraw all other applications.
story:
The guidance counselor's office smelled of coffee and old paper, and the radiator under the window ticked like a slow clock. Alicia sat across from Mr. Lee's desk with the Early Decision agreement in front of her, the signature line blank, a pen lying beside it like something she was supposed to know how to pick up. The deadline was Friday. It was Tuesday.

"You've been staring at that page for ten minutes," Mr. Lee said. He did not sound impatient. He sounded like a man who had watched many students stare at that page. "You don't have to decide in this room. But you do have to decide by Friday."

"I want to," Alicia said. "Decide, I mean." She turned the paper over, as though the back might be more encouraging. On the front, in a paragraph she had read four times, it said that Early Decision was a binding commitment. She had looked the word up on Monday night, then closed the laptop and eaten a bowl of cereal standing at the counter.

From her seat she could see the corkboard by the door, layered with years of college pennants and a faded poster of a lighthouse that said START NOW. Down the hall, the late bell rang, and footsteps thinned out, and then it was very quiet except for the radiator. Lana appeared in the doorway with her backpack on one shoulder, holding two printouts the way a person holds evidence.

"Mr. Lee said I could come in," Lana said, and sat down without waiting for an answer. She put the printouts on the desk between them. "Alicia, I did the aid estimator for you. Three schools. Look."

Alicia looked. The numbers were different at every school, and none of them were the same as the number her mother had guessed out loud last week, standing at the sink, drying a pot with a dish towel and not looking at her. The trouble was simple and enormous: Early Decision meant she would get an answer from this one school in December, and only from this one school, and she would have to say yes or no before anyone else had offered her anything.

"Binding," Lana said, tapping the paragraph. "If they take you and the aid is okay, you enroll. And you pull every other application. That's what it is."

"I know what it is," Alicia said, and immediately regretted the sharpness, because she hadn't known, not really, until Lana said it out loud in Mr. Lee's office with the printouts as proof that other schools would have offered other numbers. She had been prevaricating with herself for two weeks, telling her mother it was a strategy question, telling Mr. Lee she needed to think about her essay, when really she was afraid of finding out.

Lana, for her part, had spent the whole fall telling anyone who would listen that Early Decision was for dilettantes, people who treated applying like a game of chance. She had said so at lunch on Monday, splitting her cookie in half with surgical fairness. Now she watched Alicia read the printouts and changed her mind in the time it took to do it. "Actually," Lana said quietly, "I get it now. You love the school. It's just that love doesn't come with a price tag attached until December."

Mr. Lee did not lecture. He turned his monitor so they could see the regular decision deadlines, all of them in January, comfortably after December, and then he slid a second form across the desk, the ordinary kind, the non-binding kind. He said only, "You have more than one option in front of you. That's all I'll say." He got up to refill his coffee and left the two of them alone with the forms.

Alicia read the paragraph one more time, the whole binding architecture of it, the single answer arriving in December, the withdrawal of everything else, the condition of acceptable aid. Then she thought about her mother at the sink, and the pot drying in its towel, and the estimator numbers on Lana's printouts that no one could promise would be matched. She picked up the pen. She did not sign the Early Decision agreement. She signed the regular decision form, and her hand was steady, and she understood that she was choosing uncertainty on purpose, a whole extra spring of it, in exchange for the right to compare.

Later, in the parking lot, Lana asked whether she felt bad about it, giving up the better odds. Alicia considered the question honestly, the way she was trying to consider things now. "I don't know yet," she said. "Ask me in April." Lana laughed, and they walked toward the bus stop, and the printouts were folded in Alicia's pocket, where she could feel their edge through the fabric.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The antiderivative of 1 over x is the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x, which fills the one gap the power rule leaves.
story:
The library had one table by the west windows, and Felix had claimed it at three o'clock with a Calculus textbook, two pencils, and the private conviction that integrals were a personal insult. He had a quiz on Friday and a scholarship deadline in six weeks, and between those two facts sat the area under a curve, which he was supposed to find by reversing the power rule. That part worked. He raised the exponent by one, divided by the new exponent, and the areas of x squared and x cubed and even x to the negative one half all surrendered without much fuss. Then he turned the page and met the integral of one over x, and his method collapsed in the space of a single line.

He wrote it out anyway. One over x was x to the negative one. Raise the exponent: x to the zero. Divide by the new exponent: divide by zero. He stared at the fraction as though it might apologize. Faris, two chairs down, leaned over the edge of his own notebook and said, "You've gone very still."

"I've divided by zero."

"Congrats. New phylum of mistake." Faris was not being cruel, exactly; he classified errors the way other people classified birds, with affection and no mercy. He was at the table for his own reasons, which had less to do with calculus than with the fact that Willow came to the library on Wednesdays. Felix had watched him arrange his highlighters toward her usual chair with the care of a man setting a table for someone important.

Willow arrived at half past three carrying a crate of yearbook proofs, which she set down across from Faris with an efficiency that disabused Felix of any notion that the table belonged to him. She had a deadline of her own, the printer needed the sports spreads by five, and she spread the photographs across the wood like a weather system. "Don't mind me," she said, already minding everything.

Felix went back to the gap. The power rule had worked for every exponent he could think of except this one, which meant the one over x case was not a footnote but a hole in the method itself, a door that looked like a wall. He did what he had watched Mr. Sato's better students do, which was open the back of the book and look for the shape of the thing he didn't understand. In the table of integrals, third line down, he found it: the antiderivative of one over x was the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x. Not a power at all. A completely different animal, waiting in the answer key as though it had been obvious all along.

"So it's the one gap the power rule leaves," he said, mostly to the page.

Faris looked over. "Say that again."

"One over x. The power rule leaves exactly that one gap, and the logarithm fills it." Felix copied the line into his notebook, then copied it again, because his hand did not yet believe it. He tested it against a number, the way you nudge a loose tooth: the natural log of the absolute value of x, and its derivative came back as one over x. It held. He sat with the strangeness of it for a moment, that the curve whose area he wanted could not be caught by the same net that caught all the others, and that mathematics had apparently known this and simply not told him.

Willow held up two photographs of the swim team, the same eight boys in slightly different blurs. "Which one says state semifinals and which one says Tuesday practice nobody remembers?"

"The blurry one," said Faris, with an effusion of confidence that Felix found unjustified, since the photos were identical to him.

"Everyone says the blurry one." She chose the sharp one on principle and clipped it to her spread. Felix noticed she had left a second chair's worth of space beside her, and noticed that Faris had noticed, and that neither of them was going to do anything about it, which was its own kind of gap, though not one with a table in the back of any book.

He worked three more integrals while the light moved across the proofs and Willow's spreads went into a folder one page at a time. The logarithm kept appearing, absolute value brackets and all, patient as a friend who had been sitting in the library all along. At some point Faris leaned back and asked, in a voice pitched slightly too casually, whether Willow needed help carrying the crate to the printer. Willow looked up at him over the folder.

"You could hold the door," she said.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: On a closed interval, a function's largest value can occur at an endpoint where the derivative is not zero, so the endpoints must be checked as well.
story:
Maria got the quiz back on a Tuesday, folded once lengthwise so the mark faced inward, which was a habit she had developed sometime in grade ten and never examined. Ms. Ricci had written four out of seven beside the last question, and beside that, in red, a single sentence: you never tested the ends of the interval. Maria read it three times during the announcements, then folded the paper again and put it in the front pocket of her binder, the one that was supposed to be impermeable to loose sheets but mostly just bent them.

The question had asked for the largest value of a function on the interval from zero to eight. Maria had taken the derivative, set it equal to zero, found the critical point at x equals three, and written down the value there with a small flourish of certainty. She remembered the flourish. She remembered, too, Mia leaning over from the next desk and whispering something about the ends, and Maria shaking her head, mouthing max means the top of the hill, and turning her paper over before Mia could say the rest.

At lunch she found Mia at the window table in the cafeteria, sun coming off the parking lot behind her so that she had to squint. Melodie was there too, unpacking a container of rice with the concentration of someone preempting any request to share it. Maria put the quiz flat on the table between the container and Mia's elbow.

"Four out of seven," Maria said.

Mia looked at the page without touching it. "The answer's eight," she said. "The function at the right endpoint."

"I got the critical point."

"I know. I tried to tell you." Mia said it without triumph, which somehow made it worse, and Melodie paused with her fork halfway to her mouth, watching them both the way she watched arguments in the hallway, as physiology rather than drama, something with causes she could name if she cared to.

Maria turned back to the question herself, covering the red sentence with her thumb as though that would help her see freshly. The function rose to its peak at x equals three and then fell, gently at first, then faster, all the way to x equals eight, and at eight the value was eight, which was higher than the value at the peak. She had drawn the hill in her head and never drawn what came after the hill. She had believed that the top of a hill meant the top of everything.

"It's not even that I didn't know," she said. "It's that I was so sure."

"That's usually how it works," Melodie said, and went back to her rice.

After school, the hallway outside Ms. Ricci's room smelled of whiteboard marker and the mop the caretaker had left leaning against the trophy case. Ms. Ricci was stacking quizzes, the same quizzes, into a folder. Maria stood in the doorway with her binder against her chest.

"I'm not asking for the marks back," she said. "I want to know how I should have seen it."

Ms. Ricci looked up. "Seen what?"

"The end. Before the end."

Ms. Ricci set the folder down and for a moment Maria thought she was about to launch into one of her speeches, the kind that started with the word mathematically and ended with the bell. Instead she pulled a clean sheet toward her and drew a long horizontal line, and then a curve that climbed, peaked, descended, and kept descending until it crossed the line's far edge.

"Closed interval," Ms. Ricci said, tapping both ends. "You check these."

"I did the derivative right, though."

"You did the derivative right."

Maria took the sheet and held it. Somewhere down the corridor a door slammed and the mop bucket rang against the tile, and she thought of her father, who had wanted her to be a swimmer because she had been good at it at eleven, and who had watched her quit at fourteen with a face she still couldn't read. She had been sure about the hill then, too. She had been sure that leaving a thing at its peak was the same as winning it.

She walked home the long way, past the field where cross-country practice had already started, small figures looping the track in the fading light. At her desk she redid the question from the beginning. Derivative, zero, critical point, and then, in a column she ruled herself with the edge of the quiz, the value at the left end and the value at the right end, and a circle around the larger one. She looked at the circle for a while, undecided about whether it made her feel better or worse.

Her phone buzzed. Mia: did she give you the marks back. Maria typed no, then deleted it, then typed i got a piece of paper with a line on it instead, and sent that. She propped the drawing against her lamp where the curve's long decline was visible from across the room, and opened her notebook to tomorrow's homework.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, a new employee fills out Form W-4 so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck.
story:
The fluorescent lights of Henderson's Grocery made every apple look polished to a shine, and Noemie stood at the customer service counter trying to look like someone who belonged behind it. The manager, a heavyset man with a lanyard that said TRAIN THE TEAM, had already asked her three questions, and she had answered them the way she had practiced in the mirror: available weekends, good with people, responsible. Aleah had coached her on that last one. "Nobody's responsible at sixteen," Aleah had said, laughing. "But say it like you invented it."

He slid a folder across the counter. "Paperwork," he said. "Fill it out tonight, bring it back tomorrow, and you can start bagging Saturday." He was already turning toward a spill announcement over the intercom, so she didn't get to ask what she most wanted to ask, which was whether the money would come before the end of the month.

At home she spread the forms on her bed. Name, address, Social Security number, which her mother recited from the kitchen without looking up from the dishes. Then the last page stopped her cold. Form W-4, it said at the top, and below that, a grid of boxes and instructions she read three times without anything clicking into place. She understood that the form mattered, and she understood nothing else.

She texted her mother, who was ten feet away and famously slow with her phone. What's a W-4. Then, when no reply came, she carried the form into the kitchen and set it on the counter beside the dish rack.

Her mother dried her hands and looked at it for a long moment. "That's the form a new employee fills out so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck," she said. "Your father did one at the plant." She tapped the top line. "Everybody starting a job does this. It's normal." Then she went back to the sink, and Noemie was left holding a pen over a page that had suddenly become the least of her problems, because her mother had said starting a job in a voice that was careful and light, as if neither of them remembered the last conversation they'd had about money.

That conversation had happened three weeks ago, in this same kitchen, and it had ended with her mother counting the grocery envelope twice and saying, quietly, that thirty-six dollars was missing. Noemie had said maybe the cashier made a mistake. That was the version she'd told Aleah, too, along with a version about why she wanted the job: concert tickets, independence, something to put on a college application someday. Aleah had believed her completely. Noemie had discovered that lying to a friend was easier than lying to a mother, and she hadn't decided yet what that made her. Not a liar exactly. Something more specialized.

She filled in the boxes slowly, copying her address letter by letter, and when she got to the part about allowances she stopped again and texted Cory, whose older brother had worked at the movie theater all last summer. do u know what to put on the W4. Cory replied five minutes later with a shrug emoji and the words ask ur mom, and Noemie stared at the screen feeling both ridiculous and strangely cornered, as if the form itself were an auxiliary exam she hadn't studied for, a second test hiding behind the first.

At school the next morning she found Aleah at the lockers and told her, casually, that the job was real, that she'd start Saturday. Aleah hugged her. "Tickets," Aleah said, holding up two fingers. Noemie opened her mouth, and what came out surprised them both. "Not tickets," she said. "Something else. I'll tell you when I can." Aleah's eyebrows went up, but she let it go, which was either trust or laziness, and Noemie didn't ask which.

Saturday morning she walked to Henderson's with the completed forms in a folder against her chest. She had decided she would give the first paychecks to her mother without explaining, just put the money in the envelope on the counter and say, count it. Whether her mother would understand, or forgive, or even mention it again, Noemie couldn't know, and she turned that uncertainty over the whole way there like a coin she couldn't stop flipping. At the service entrance the manager took the folder, glanced through the pages, and gave a small nod. "W-4's good," he said. "Register three. Follow me."

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: Sonata form has three main sections: the exposition presents the themes, the development works them through other keys, and the recapitulation brings them back.
story:
The garage smelled of engine oil and cold coffee, and Alexander had until seven o'clock, which was the hour Mr. Whitaker's ensemble would open with the Mozart, and the hour by which Alexander had to hand in a marked analysis or lose the last credit that kept his scholarship file intact. He had the score spread across the hood of his mother's car, held flat by a socket wrench and a coffee can of screws, and he had three colours of sticky notes, yellow, blue, green, fanned beside it like cards he was afraid to play.

"You're doing this in a garage," Loik said from the doorway, letting in the cold. "On a car."

"The house is full of my aunt's moving boxes. And the piano's here anyway." There was a piano against the back wall, an upright that had come with the house, its tuning somewhere between uncertain and optimistic. Alexander had been playing the opening bars on it since noon, stopping each time at the same measure, the one where the music seemed to change its mind.

Edith came in behind Loik carrying a thermos and her own copy of the score, dog-eared at the edges. "I finished mine last night," she said, not unkindly, which made it worse. "Took me four hours. You have two."

"I know how long I have." He set the yellow note above the first page. That much he trusted: the opening, the part everyone could hum, belonged at the start. He pressed it down and the glue caught the cold metal of the hood badly, and he had to hold it a moment until it stayed.

"Okay, so walk me through what you actually know," Edith said, pouring coffee into the thermos lid and handing it to him. "Say it out loud. That's how I figured mine out."

He played the first eight bars, the theme arriving the way a person walks into a room, confident, unmistakable. "That's a theme," he said. "That part presents itself. It's not shy about it." He played on, and somewhere around the double bar the music lifted and slid, the same tune but wearing different light, and he stopped with his hands still on the keys.

"That's the second one," Edith said. "It changed key. That's the give-away. When the themes come back in a different key, that whole stretch is called the exposition." She said it lightly, checking him rather than teaching him, the way she quizzed French verbs on the bus.

"Both themes. All of it, up to there." Alexander wrote on the yellow note, "first and second themes," and set it above the double bar. His hand was steadier than he expected. "So what's the blue one for?"

Loik had drifted to the piano and picked out the melody with one finger, slow and glacial, until Alexander could not stand it and reached over to correct the fingering. Loik grinned and moved his finger to the next phrase, and Alexander went still, because the phrase was wrong, and then right, and then wrong again in a way that was deliberate, the tune pulled apart and restated somewhere it didn't belong.

"That bit's doing something different," Loik said. "It's not giving you the theme. It's taking it apart."

Alexander followed it in the score with his pencil. The music wandered, the themes surfaced in keys they had no business visiting, argued with themselves, drifted. "That's it," he said, and his voice came out louder than he meant. "That's the development. It works the themes through other keys. That's what the blue is for." He wrote on the blue note and stuck it at the start of the wandering, and then, hunting, played forward until the music stopped wandering, until the opening theme returned, whole, home, and he slapped the blue note's edge to mark where the working-through ended.

Edith leaned over the hood. "And then?"

"Then it comes back." He played the return, the theme walking into the room again, same tune, but this time staying where it began. "The recapitulation brings them back." He wrote on the green note, held it above the final pages, and did not press it down.

"Three notes, three sections, done," Loik said. "Two of those are on the hood. Car's not going to grade it."

But Alexander kept his thumb off the green note. Because the return, when he played it, was not identical. The second theme came back and did not change key the way it had the first time, and he could hear that it mattered, and he could not have said why. He said so. "I can mark the edges. I can't promise the middle is right. There's a page in the development where I'd bet on either of two bars."

Edith looked at the clock on the wall, which was ten minutes fast and always had been. "Hand it in like that. Mark your doubt with a pencil note. Mr. Whitaker said he'd rather see a question we can defend than an answer we can't."

"Since when does he show clemency?"

"Since the quiz on modulation, which half the class failed and he reweighted. Ask him yourself in an hour."

Alexander pressed the green note down. He took the pencil and wrote, small, in the margin where the two possible bars met: "not sure here, could be either." Then he gathered the pages, squared them against the piano's lid, and found that his hands had stopped shaking somewhere in the last ten minutes without his noticing.

"Give me a ride," Edith said. "Or we're both late."

He pocketed the car keys, and Loik pulled the garage door up into the last of the light.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Malcolm Gladwell's 2008 book Outliers popularized the '10,000-hour rule', though Ericsson later said the quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours.
story:
The guitar had a crack along its body that Ms. López had covered with tape shaped like a bird, and Alexandre held it the way he imagined a person would hold something borrowed and precious, which it was. Fifth period, the music classroom emptied of everyone except him and Jaelyn, who had claimed the piano bench as her homework desk since September. He pressed his left hand into a C chord and produced a sound like a door refusing to open.

"You started too late," Jaelyn said, not looking up from her calculus. "Kieran said the same thing when you signed up. Ten thousand hours. That's the rule."

"Whose rule?"

"Malcolm Gladwell. He wrote a book in 2008, Outliers. Ten thousand hours of practice and you get good. Kieran's been playing since he was six, so he's got, what, half of it banked already. You've got nothing." She finally turned. "You're seventeen. It's pointless."

He strummed again and the chord held, wobbling, but held. Outside, the marching band drilled on the field, their formations visible through the blinds like a diagram being erased and redrawn.

That night he did what he always did when a number was thrown at him: he looked it up. His phone screen lit the dark of his room while his father's television murmured through the wall. Gladwell, 2008, the ten thousand hours, the famous rule. But underneath the summaries there was the man the rule had come from, a researcher named Ericsson, saying later that it was the quality of the practice that mattered more than any fixed number of hours. Alexandre read that sentence twice. It did not say the number was wrong, exactly. It said something else mattered more. He lay back with the guitar flat on his chest, not practicing, just holding it, feeling the difference between those two ideas like the difference between a fence and a gate.

He thought about the cello. In fourth grade his mother had rented one for a semester, and he had quit because the other kids said the case looked like a coffin and he had decided, at nine, that being seen mattered more than being heard. He could not remember the cello's sound at all, only the case, only the hallway, only his own parochial certainty about what people would think. That was the choice he was weighing now, in the dark, on a school night, with a taped-up guitar on his chest: whether the reason to quit was real this time or just a coffin-shaped story he was telling himself.

The next day he found Kieran in the hallway by the vending machines, the one place in school where Kieran's opinions came cheap and abundant, and Kieran being something of an epicure in that regard, sampling every controversy.

"You're not seriously still doing the guitar," Kieran said. "Do the math. Ten thousand hours. You'd be thirty-something before you caught up to me."

"Gladwell got it from Ericsson," Alexandre said. "And Ericsson later said the quality of the practice matters more than any fixed number of hours."

Kieran popped open a soda. "So practice better, I guess."

"Or start late and practice better."

"Same thing."

But it was not the same thing, and Alexandre knew it even while failing to say how. Still, he went to Ms. López after class and asked her what practicing better would actually look like, and she said, "Slower than you want to," and put a metronome on the stand set to a speed that felt insulting. He played eight notes. He played them again. The eighth mistake he caught before he made it, which had never happened before, and something in him sat up.

For three weeks this was his life: the taped guitar, the insulting metronome, the same eight notes until they stopped being notes and became something his hands simply knew. Jaelyn stopped doing calculus at the piano and started doing it on the floor beside him, which he understood to be her version of an apology without either of them naming it. Kieran drifted in once, watched for four minutes, and said, "You're doing the same thing over and over."

"That's the point," Alexandre said.

"Sounds boring."

It was not boring, though Alexandre could not have explained why without sounding like a person who had been captivated by eight notes, which he had been. He was also, he had to admit, still slow, still clumsy, still seventeen with no banked hours, and when the winter recital sign-up sheet went up, he stood in front of it for a long time with a pen uncapped. Ericsson had not promised anything. Quality over quantity was a principle, not a guarantee, and Alexandre could not close the gap between principle and outcome in his head. He remembered the cello case and the hallway and the ease of that old quitting. He wrote his name down.

The night of the recital, backstage, Kieran tuned his own guitar with the calm of someone whose hours were all paid for. "You nervous?" he asked.

"Yes."

"Good," Kieran said. "I'm never nervous anymore. I kind of miss it." He said this looking at the floor, and Alexandre understood that this, too, was a kind of giving up, though he did not say so. Ms. López poked her head through the curtain, said his name, and Alexandre walked out. The lights were too bright to see Jaelyn or anyone. He found the frets in the dark of his own hands, waited one breath past the point of wanting to begin, and began.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Under US federal law, workers aged 16 and 17 have no limit on working hours but may not be employed in jobs the Department of Labor has declared hazardous.
story:
Maika set the kitchen chair three feet from the couch, the way the career booklet said to sit, and Kohl lowered himself onto the cushion with a legal pad and a terrible posture.

"Interview for a part-time job," he read. "Question one. Tell me about yourself."

"I'm Maika. I'm seventeen. I want this job because." She stopped. Her eyes had drifted to the window, where the neighbor's sprinkler ticked across the lawn in its slow arc.

"Hey. Eyes. That's the whole point of tonight."

"I know." She reset her chin. "I'm Maika, I'm seventeen, and I learn fast." Better, but her voice went up at the end as if asking permission.

Kohl wanted the counter job at Osvaldo's himself. He'd said so twice on the walk over, casually, the way you mention rain. If she bombed Saturday's interview, the position would still be open, and he could take it without anyone calling it a betrayal. She had decided not to think about that, and to sublimate what she couldn't stop thinking into repetition, drilling answers until they had edges.

"Question two. Why should we hire you?"

"Because I show up. Because I'm careful." She held his gaze this time, and he nodded once, writing nothing.

The third question was the one that mattered. He read it with a small grin. "The manager asks if you can close the deli station Saturday nights. Running the meat slicer."

"Sure," she said, reflexive.

"Wait." He flipped the pad over. On the back he'd copied something off his phone. "My uncle got sent home from a grocery job for exactly this. Sixteen and seventeen-year-olds, there's no limit on how many hours we can work. None. But the Department of Labor has jobs it calls hazardous, and we can't be put in those."

"The slicer's hazardous?"

"Uncle says it's on the list. Meat slicers, paper balers, that kind of thing."

"So they can schedule me all night," she said slowly, "just not at that machine."

"That's the whole shape of it."

Ms. Romano had told her something similar once, in her cluttered kitchen across the fence, though Maika hadn't understood at the time what it was for. Now she understood it was for exactly this: the moment a manager, maybe not unkindly, maybe just busy, asked a seventeen-year-old to do something she shouldn't be asked to do. Her mother's advice had been simpler. Take whatever they offer. Don't make waves. Her mother's milieu was one where rules were things that happened to you, and Maika had grown up treating that as wisdom. But the two ideas could be braided, she thought, standing at the kitchen counter while Kohl poured them both water. She could want the job badly and still say no to the slicer. She could be grateful and not be a doormat. What she couldn't yet tell was whether the manager at Osvaldo's would respect the distinction or would simply move on to an applicant who never said no. That part stayed dark, and she let it stay dark.

She practiced the answer four times. The first attempt came out like a legal brief. The second came out apologetic. The third, Kohl said, sounded like she was accusing him of a crime.

The fourth went like this: "I can close Saturday nights, and any night, honestly. The one thing I can't run is the meat slicer. At my age it's a hazardous job under federal law. I'm happy to do everything around it, and I'll learn the station when I'm old enough."

Kohl put the pad down. "That was actually good."

"You sound surprised."

"You weren't looking at the floor once."

She checked the clock. Nine-forty. The interview was at ten on Saturday, and between now and then was school, and her mother's shift, and whatever her mother would say about turning down slicer duty. Kohl gathered his pad and his phone, and at the door he paused, hand on the frame.

"Saturday morning, before you go," he said. "I'll run the questions again. All of them."

"Even though you want the job."

"Even though." He shrugged into his jacket. "If you get it by being better at interviews, that's fair. If I get it because you choked, that's nothing."

After he left she moved the chair back to the table and stood a moment in the quiet kitchen, the sprinkler still ticking outside. Then she picked up her phone and typed a note to herself: hours, unlimited; slicer, no. She read it twice, put the phone face down, and went to rehearse her answer one more time, alone, straight into the dark window where her own reflection held her eyes.
